speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I wish to direct a question to the Minister of National Revenue. Harvest is now due in Canada and farm help is very difficult to get. Many of these workers will come as volunteers from towns and cities and work part time, perhaps in the afternoon or evening. Will the wages paid to these voluntary farm workers be subject to the income tax, and if so, what part does the farmer play in it?

speakeroldname: Hon. C. W. G. GIBSON (Minister of National Revenue):
speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
subtopic: VOLUNTARY WORKERS-INCOME TAX DEDUCTIONS
speechtext: All wages are subject to income tax, but as to wages paid to temporary help on farms, such as students working in the summer, the farmers are notified that no deductions need be made in such cases where the amount earned during the summer will not come up to the taxable level. That is, the farmers do not have to make deductions in the case of temporary help engaged for short periods during the summer.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
I have a number of statements I wish to make; but, in answer to the question just raised, 1 think the suggestion made by the hon. member for Qu'Appelle that 1 should obtain the post office addresses of men who are employed on the Qu'Appelle Valley projects in connection with surveys, I shall have to get those addresses from the Regina office; I have not got them up to date. There are two or three statements which I agreed to make the other evening when we were on the war appropriation which do affect somewhat these estimates as well, and one which I have been asked to make as a result of statements in connection with the movement of grain.
A Canadian Press report appeared, following the discussions the other day, in these words:
Hon. J. G. Gardiner, agricultural minister, told the commons last night that due to the lack of transportation facilities less than one hundred million bushels of Canadian wheat have been moved to the United States, although there is a market for two hundred million bushels.
The word there should not be "wheat" but "coarse grains" or "feed grains." The matter under discussion was not wheat, but feed grain.
The dispatch continues:
Replying to questions from M. J. Coldwell, C.C.F. leader-
I do not know, Mr. Chairman, whether you can hear me; I can hardly hear myself.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Order.
Supply-Agriculture
Does that "feed grain" include wheat?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
I was talking about oats and barley. To make it absolutely plain, when I spoke of 200 million bushels I was not talking of wheat at all; it was oats and barley.
Replying to questions from M. J. Coldwell, C.C.F. leader, Mr. Gardiner said both Canada and the United States were handicapped by lack of railway cars and lake shipping facilities to take Canadian wheat to American markets.
Some grain ears were made available to Canadian railways to carry wheat to the head of the lakes, whence to be shipped to United States buyers, particularly in Maine and other eastern states.
The point is this, that before completing that statement the other evening I said that the railway companies were doing a particularly good job under all the circumstances. That does not appear in the press report. As a result of this report going out I had communications from both the railways pointing out the job that they had done up to the moment, and I would like to place on the record the substance of that report, so that what has been done will be known:
Grain of all kinds moved from lake head since April 26, 1943, by water to July 5, 1943, 111,838,000 bushels as against 92,408,000 bushels from March 30, 1942, or 19,430,000 bushels more in 1943 than in 1942. That is of all grain, wheat and feed grain as well, they have moved this year 19,430,000 bushels more in the same period of time, that is from the opening of the lakes up to the present time, than they did a year ago.
Then, loaded at head of the lakes for all rail movement to eastern ports, August 1, 1942, to date, 30,000 carloads as against 19,200 carloads in 1941-42.
To-day held unloaded on track, Canadian Pacific, 3,000 cars at lake head, 3,000 cars ' at Winnipeg, 3,500 at other points, making a total of 9,500 cars on track: Canadian National, 2,000 cars at lake head; 1,854 cars at other points, making a total of 3,854.
Then, to American ports, Buffalo, 33,673,000 bushels, and to other points, 19,172,000 bushels, or 52,845.000 bushels have been moved to the United States ports.
The total of 111,838,000 bushels is divided as follows: United States ports, 52,845,000 bushels; Canadian ports, 58,993,000 bushels.
I repeat that that is since April 26, 1943 down to the present. I would like to repeat what I said on the previous occasion, with these facts before the committee, that we consider that a particularly good job has been done by the railways. But the fact still remains that we have 200,000,000 bushels of oats and barley from last year's crop
[The Chairman.]
which ought to be moved out of western Canada and should have been moved by some means if it were at all possible before the new crop came in, and hon. members can see the importance of getting that down between now and the middle of August. As I stated the other day, the problem is obviously a transportation problem, and I am not blaming the railways for that; I am only saying that we have an unusually large amount of feed grain in this country which we should have liked to see moved to the United States and eastern Canada, and so far no one has found it possible to move it.
In what part of the provinces is most of this feed grain?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: It is all over the three prairie provinces. As my hon. friend knows, a very considerable part of it Is still out on the fields, not under cover. What I am trying to do is to overcome some of the things that are being stated. For example, I have here an editorial which appeared in the Financial Post which came to my table just this morning, entitled "He takes credit from heaven". The article goes on to say that I am continuously drumming away about this surplus of feed grain that we have and implying that there is no trouble about feeding the people of Canada next winter, and that it was heaven that gave us this crop and we ought to be more concerned about it. Well, right at the moment I am concerned about getting a place to put the next crop so that it will not be lying out under heaven but will be under a roof some place, and I would like the assistance of the Financial Post and a few other of these periodicals in getting that done rather than saying all the time that we want something else done.

The grain exchange are
not worrying very much about it, judging from the way they are boosting the price.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: The grain exchange can make money only by getting the grain transported from one place to some other place. They cannot get money while it is lying on the farm and not moving, and therefore I presume they are as anxious as anyone else to get that grain moving. Everybody in the west wants to get it moving and we want the help of everyone towards this end.

How many hundred
million bushels are lying there?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
All the grain we have fed in Canada before amounted to half a billion bushels of oats and barley. Last year

Supply-Agriculture
we produced a billion bushels. In other words, we produced twice as much as we had fed [DOT] before, and we agreed last fall to try to put
200.000.	000 bushels of that into the United States. That would still leave us with
300.000.	000 bushels more than we had the year before to feed all our live stock, and we wanted to keep that as a reserve. To date we have not been able to move half of it and we are within a month of our new crop. I would emphasize that we do want the assistance of all the shipping people, all the railway people and all the newspapers in Canada to try to get that grain moved to the United States where they tell us there is a shortage of feed grain. That is the only way the farmers can get money out of it.

The United States
could take all of it if it could be transported. The only difficulty is lack of transportation.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: Yes, lack of sufficient transportation. We are not criticizing the railways. Somebody is asking the railways to move munitions, guns and other supplies, and in spite of that they are moving more grain than they did before. The problem of the farmers in getting their stock fed involves the moving of that grain out of these piles on the fields to the places where the stock is, and there is only one way of doing that, namely, by railway and boat.
Is there also a demand in eastern Canada which cannot be filled because of lack of transportation?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
Yes. There is a demand.
I do not know that there is any great suffering at the moment, but unless we can get a very considerable volume of that grain moved this summer into storages there will be trouble next winter. That trouble will not have anything to do with what heaven does this year with the crop. That grain is there and we wTant it moved to the east and put into storage elevators, and an order in council has already been passed by the government putting up money to cover the extra cost.
What cost?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: Any extra cost to hold the grain between the time it is shipped down and the time it would be shipped under ordinary circumstances.

Is there not another difficulty in the financing of the grain to hold it in storage? There is not a sufficiency of funds available, particularly among the farmers, to purchase the grain and keep it in storage until next winter's feeding.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: An order has already been passed and there is an order now under consideration, which I hope will be passed in some form in due course and which is known to the trade and others who will be handling this business, and that will take care of the problem of providing for grain being moved down. So far as the financing of that kind of thing is concerned, the trade is .prepared to finance it provided the government is nulling to take care of the extra charges that would be involved by reason of shipping it now instead of waiting until next January or February, and we are attempting to provide for that under the arrangements that are being made. I wish to make that clear to the committee before we discuss the other statement I had intended putting on the record.

Is there an abundance of grain available in Fort William to people who need it? I was talking to one dealer a few days ago and he said he had difficulty at that time in getting sufficient oats or barley from Fort William for his customers.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: There was difficulty last winter, in spite of these figures which indicate that very much more was being moved; notwithstanding the difficult winter we had, the railways moved more grain than they had been accustomed to moving-very much more -owing to the fact that there is much more live stock being fed this year. In addition there is a poor grain crop in the eastern part of Canada; at any rate they anticipate a poor crop because of the late seeding. Because we are afraid of that we have made every possible arrangement and everyone is trying to cooperate in getting that grain put down here. Moreover, we are trying to develop some means of encouraging the farmers to take it from the feeder and put it into their own storage. All that is involved in the orders I spoke of a moment ago, and we believe that a very considerable amount of grain will be moved down before the freeze-up this fall, and put into storage here, to supply the farmers. It is true, as represented to the hon. member for Souris, that there will be different localities in the east that will now have trouble because this grain did not get down in sufficient quantities last winter or the early part of this season.

I believe I raised the point the other day about the anticipation of a shortage of feed in Ontario and eastern Canada, and also the question of the price that will be charged to feeders in eastern Canada. If it is brought down and left in the hands of the trade the trade can perhaps
Supply-Agriculture

charge the farmers what they like. There is a ceiling on feed grain, but after it is processed and made into chop for feeding, is any precaution being taken to see that the farmer does not pay a veiy high price for it? That would probably come under the wartime prices and trade board, from the point of view of prices.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: My understanding is that the grains themselves are all under a ceiling and it is impossible for dealers to collect freight on the grain shipped from Fort William unless they abide absolutely by these regulations. In addition to that, there are ceilings on such things as mill feeds, and I understand that there are ceilings on the other feeds as well. I did not want to be too certain about that, but there are ceilings so far as our activities with them are concerned. They cannot collect freight unless they sell with the price margins as between what they obtain the product for and what it cost to market it. We have to be satisfied on that question, before paying freight which does establish a ceiling.
So long as the farmers are protected I do not care. That is all I am worrying about.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: That is what we are trying to do, and if there are cases where that is not being done I should like to have a report regarding them.
Would it not'facilitate matters with regard to this whole situation if the grain board handled all this grain instead of letting the grain exchange in Winnipeg operate?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
Of course if the grain board were going to handle it all they would have to set up agencies all over eastern Canada. I do not want to enter into a discussion of the question whether it is better to have grain handled by a government board or otherwise, but the facilities are all set up in eastern Canada, through feed dealers at every small point throughout the farming area, and we have been utilizing that machinery to distribute this grain. They have had their contacts with different grain companies from which they get their grain, and the business is being done much in the manner in which it was done before the war. But it is being done under regulations, and we are keeping a check on the margins that do exist between the cost of grain and the selling price of the product. We are keeping a check on these margins with the idea of keeping down the cost of producing food in Canada. Our object is to keep down the price of feed to the farmer in eastern 
Canada, and so far as it is necessary to take * care of the western farmer we are allowing him to participate in the price of any grain which is shipped out of Canada, spreading that participation over all those who sell oats or barley in western Canada, whether it is shipped east or to the United States. So that the man who supplies an eastern Canadian farmer, under the ceiling, will eventually get the same price for his grain as the man who supplies the United States market with grain.
If the grain board does not ship grain out of Canada, how will the farmer participate in that?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: The grain board issues a permit to anyone who ships grain out, and they have to pay the difference between the Canadian market and the United States market.
But that does not include the higher grades of wheat.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: No; the higher grades of wheat are selling in the United States higher than the market price in Canada. As to wheat that has been delivered to the board, the advance is the same whether it is finally sold in the United States or not. If it is sold at a profit in the United States, participation certificates take care of the producer's interests.

But grain is paying a dollar in the grain exchange at Winnipeg, or, as the minister said the other day, $1.02. If the board is handling it, whatever was received from the United States would go direct to the farmer.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
One has to remember
that the farmers always deliver their grain to the wheat board as long as the advance paid by the wheat board is higher than the market price. And up until a certain date practically all, if not all the wheat, was delivered to the board. Then at a certain time the price rose above 90 cents. In fact it has gone up to about $1.02. Since that time practically all the grain is being delivered to the trade. That is just a choice that is made by the farmer; it is not made by the government. They must make a choice of one or two things. They can either deliver the wheat to the board and get the ninety cents advance, taking advantage of the participation certificate for collection later, or they can deliver to the trade. They have their reasons for delivering to the trade. I do not wish to discuss them at the moment. But the great majority of them, as soon as the price goes above the advance, deliver to the trade. The trade has been selling that wheat

Supply-Agriculture
as they bought it, and probably some of it is offered by the board on the market. The wheat which is delivered by the board on the market will be getting ten cents a bushel to go toward participation certificates. But the wheat which goes to the line companies will be sold by the line companies at whatever the market is. They will buy at whatever the market is, and they will sell at whatever the market is. To that extent they may make some profit, or they may make some loss, depending on how the trade goes.

But the farmer gets
nothing out of it.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
Nothing more than
what he selected when he made his choice. He may have chosen to take that price rather than the ninety cents advance.

But to-day he
is getting $1.05 in Fort William.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: Yes, I guess it has been as high as that.
It is $1.05 to-day.
It is only $1.03.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture

speechtext: The farmer in the United States is getting a better price than the farmer in Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: That is admitted by everyone.
That was the point I was making.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: The point is that so far as the Canadian dealer in wool is concerned, he can realize more at the present time, under all conditions, with our prices here, than he could on any other market. That was the point I made.
My point was that a condition should be brought about in Canada, by subsidy, or in some other way, under which we can get a price which would compare with the price in the United States.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: I understand that. There was another question asked by the hon. member for Melfort. He asked that I place on record the figures which indicated that nearly $100,000,000 had been paid to farmers in subsidies and acreage payments in one year.
The minister said there was a hundred million.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
I will deal with that too. I made the definite statement that there was nearly-or, I believe I said, pretty nearly-
8100,000,000 in acreage payments and subsidies, and I was asked .to put those figures on record. I have them here. These are the subsidies paid to agriculture in the calendar year 1942-that is, some of these amounts will relate to the 1941 crop, but they were paid in the calendar year 1942:
Prairie farm assistance	 $14,471,060
Prairie farm income	 18,175,114
Wheat acreage reduction	 32,297,670
Cheese quality payments	 1.730.919
Cheese factory subsidies	 203,732
Butter for subsidy	 7,000,933
Fluid and concentrated milk subsidy 3,846.036
Fertilizer subsidy	 975,275
Feed freight assistance	 9,832,004
Feed wheat, 8-cent drawback	 333,720
Egg price subsidy	 918,224
Subsidy on strawberries, by the wartime prices and trade board		42,233
Apple assistance (1)	 2,257,620
Beef cattle purchase, by the wartime prices and trade board (estimated)	 800,000
Fruit and vegetable subsidies to
canners	 741,000
Provincial subsidies on hogs and cheese for 1942 (estimated)		4,500,000
Total of subsidies and acreage payments	 $98,125,540
This figure, I believe the committee will agree, is nearly a hundred million dollars in one year, involved in these transactions alone. What we were discussing, at the time was the amount of money involved. The statement was made that hundreds of millions of dollars were going to industry in order to bring about and utilize to the full the production from factories for war purposes. I said it could be stated as surely that hundreds of millions had also been utilized to make possible the production and proper distribution of food supplies or farm products. Now, the figures with regard to that are round figures. I am not going to go into detail, because I am not allowed to do so in connection with these particular items. The wheat delivered by producers to the
Supply-Agriculture

wheat board involved financing to the extent of 8746,000,000 and carrying charges of one kind and another amounting to $115,000,000, making a total of $861,255,000 on the handling of wheat which passed through the wheat board. If one adds to that the $98,000,000 I have here, and another $150,000,000 which has been spent in direct subsidies through the years-the statement I have put on the record covers only one year-he will find that the total amounts to over a billion dollars. I think these figures substantiate what I said the other night, that in one way or another the assistance provided for the production and distribution of farm products has amounted to several hundreds of millions of dollars.

I think it would be a good idea if the minister would place on record the fact that in 1942, the year for which he has given figures, the farmers lost, because of not getting parity prices for wheat, something like $140,000,000. It is agreed that the parity price for wheat is $1.40 per bushel.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: I do not think the time has yet come for me to say that. As I understand it, more than half of the wheat is still on the farms. I think that the best- bank account there is in Canada to-day is a bin of wheat on the farm. What the farmer is going to get out of that wheat is not yet known, so that I am not in position to make that statement.

I was referring only to the
280,000,000 bushels which have been delivered.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
Even that is not all delivered; there is a considerable part of it still on the farms. The farmer has not yet lost money on that

I am not saying he will not lose something-so that I am not in position to make a statement as to what his position is with regard to the 1942 crop. I gave good reasons for that when I said that not very much has moved as yet. I want to emphasize what I have emphasized before, that the farmer has within his own hands the privilege of making sure as to whether he has an opportunity to get further returns on that crop. He can get a GO cent advance from the wheat board. If he believes in the pooling of wheat as a method of getting every cent there is to be got out of the wheat, he will put his wheat into the pool. If he believes he can make more money by selling it now, he will sell it now. I do not think that I or anyone else could interfere with his judgment in that matter; he will probably do what he thinks is wise.

I should like to point out the difference between the advances made to agriculture and those made to industry. The

minister has stated that hundreds of millions of dollars have been placed at the disposal of agriculture. As has been pointed out by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar, the hundreds of millions of dollars which have been placed at the disposal of industry become its property at the end of four or five years through depreciation, but the hundreds of millions of dollars which have been advanced to agriculture will be repayable to the government on the sale of the wheat. The minister mentioned some $98,000,000 which had been paid out as subsidies during 1943, but I would point out that these subsidies were not all for 1942. In many cases they were not paid to the primary producer, the farmer, but rather to the processor.
Another matter I wish to bring to the minister's attention is the question of car allotments to the elevators in western Canada. When Mr. Mclvor, chairman of the wheat board, was before the committee he stated that there had been no complaints as far as the board was concerned by the elevator companies. Since then I have received a number of telegrams and resolutions, and I think the chairman of the agriculture committee has received a number of resolutions, complaining bitterly about the allotment of cars made to the various elevator companies. It appears to me that the pool elevators are being discriminated against and are not receiving the cars they should. The result is that the producers cannot market their grain to their own elevators. I ask that something be done with respect to this.

I have had representations
made to me in connection with this matter since the meeting of the agriculture committee, and I took what I considered to be the proper course. I referred the representations that came to me to the officers of the Canadian wheat board. I received a reply a few days ago from the chairman of the board in which he stated specifically that until a certain telegram was received, I believe from the secretary of the Saskatchewan -wheat pool under date of June 8, the board had not received any complaints with respect to the distribution of cars. He considered that since no complaints had been received the policy which had been pursued during the past year was working reasonably satisfactorily. He went on to say in his letter that the officers of the Canadian wheat board had met with officers of the three wheat pools, the meeting being held in Winnipeg I think about a week or ten days ago. This matter was discussed for one or two hours, but there had not been evolved or suggested any scheme that was more workable than the one

Supply-Agriculture
in operation. The chairman of the wheat board went on to say that the managers of the three wheat pool organizations in western Canada were meeting officials of the Canadian wheat board to try to see if a more satisfactory system from the administrative point of view could be worked out. I think it is only fair to say that so far as the officers of the Canadian wheat board are concerned, they had not received any complaints with respect to the operation of the policy during the past year. Not having received any complaints, they considered that the policy was working out reasonably well. I repeat that steps are being taken to see whether a more workable scheme can be suggested. If it can be, I am sure that they will take steps to put it into operation. I think this statement is due the officers of the wheat board and the others concerned, because this problem of transportation is a most critical one.

I should like to support what has been said with respect to subsidies. While I know that arguments are advanced from time to time showing that the farmer is getting everything or almost everything that is coming to him, with the exception of wheat, I must say I cannot agree with them. I have admitted before on several occasions that the cure is in the farmers' hands. If the farmers want to organize as industry and labour have organized, if they want to demand what is coming to them, they can get their just rights. Until that is done they never will get what is coming to them.
In the early days of the wheat pool in my province we had fifty-one per cent of the farmers signed up, but in a short time inducements were placed before them and many of the farmers started to bootleg their grain. They were given an extra grade, but at the same time a certain number of bushels per load were removed by painless extraction. Until the farmers wake up to what they are being done for they will have to be satisfied with receiving less than they are entitled to.
There is one point I should like to bring to the attention of the minister in connection with the storage of the grain we hope to get in the 1943 crop. I believe in a number of cases farmers will be compelled to buy lumber to build bins in which to store their grain. At the present time the approximate cost of a bin twelve by fourteen by seven, with a shingle roof, which will hold about 1,100 bushels of wheat, is $110. But I understand that at the present time a farmer can buy only $200 worth of lumber at one time. If this is correct, as I believe it is, some provision should be made by which a
farmer may obtain enough lumber for more than two bins. In many cases additional storage space for 2,000 bushels will not be sufficient to take care of the crop during the coming year, because of the grain already in storage on the farms.

We have had some interesting information this morning; it appears that the Minister of Agriculture has taken over from the Minister of Trade and Commerce. In some parts of western Canada that would be good news; for I believe the minister would make a pretty good job of it. Several questions have been opened up this morning on which I should have liked to say something, but a great deal has been said here and a great deal more was said when we had Mr. Mclvor, the chairman of the board, before the agriculture committee, so that I do not think it is necessary to repeat wffiat has been said by other hon. members.
I should like to say a word in regard to discrimination in the allotment of cars. I believe there has been discrimination; and I believe the Minister of Trade and Commerce, who has just left the chamber, was well aware of it. On June 30 I asked the minister directly if he had received any protests with respect to this alleged discrimination, and he replied that he had not. Later I met him and had a conversation with him, and he informed me that while there was no direct charge of discrimination, he had received many protests from individuals. Again on July 2 I brought the matter to the attention of the minister, and he admitted again that he had received many protests but stated that the board was not going to pay very much attention to them. When I was home at Easter I heard many complaints in our district in this regard, and I think there is no doubt that if the distribution of cars had been handled without discrimination, a great deal more grain would have been moved and many farmers would have had a chance to get a greater portion of their quota off their hands.
Something has been said to-day with respect to the price of wheat. I have just received a note from the hon. member for Moose Jaw in which he offers to bet me that wheat will go much higher. I wish he had given me this information a few days ago. I was given a certain amount of encouragement in listening to the minister this morning, but I delivered my wheat to the board and took a participation certificate, which the minister mentioned a few moments ago. That applies to about half my crop. I could not deliver the full quota before January or the board would have had all the wheat I was allowed
Supply-Agriculture

to deliver. Fortunately or otherwise I could not get off the last four or five bushels of my quota until after Easter, and the price went up. As a matter of fact I held it until about twelve days ago, when wheat hit $1. I have been consistently advocating that the price of wheat should be SI, so that when I was able to get that price for it I thought I had better sell. Yesterday it reached $1.05, so you can see how I feel about it. However, part of it was delivered to the board under a participation certificate, which I hope may be worth another 20 cents before we are through.
Earlier this morning the minister said that the member for Qu'Appelle knew very well there was a great deal of grain in western Canada that should be under cover; and I will agree that if more cars had been made available and transportation facilities had been provided, much of that grain would have been under cover. Only this morning I received another letter from a lumber dealer in my constituency in regard to a matter which I took up with the lumber controller here in Ottawa. This is the second letter I have received from Mr. Rosborough, a pioneer lumber dealer at Grenfell, Saskatchewan. I took the matter up with the lumber controller, as I said before, but did not get very much satisfaction. This gentleman complains that he cannot get lumber to supply the farmers who want to build bins, and in the letter I received this morning he asked me to follow the matter up and see what can be done. No doubt the minister knows of many similar cases, and I suggest that he take it up with the lumber controller to see if they cannot get lumber at some of these local points so that the farmers may do the very thing the minister suggests-build bins and get their grain under cover. If he will undertake to do that it will save me the trouble of taking up the matter again with the lumber controller. In addition to the letters from this gentleman I have received several other protests from boards of trade to the effect that lumber is not available in some of these smaller towns, while in other places plenty of lumber is being supplied. The minister should go into the matter with the lumber controller and have the situation straightened out.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Order. We called an item, and while it was perfectly in order for the minister to answer questions which had been asked previously, I would beg of the committee not to go all over the items which have been passed already. I do not say that in any critical way, but I believe it to 
be the general feeling of the committee that we should keep the discussion closely to the item under consideration.
I wonder if the hon. member for Qu'Appelle would be good enough to read the note I sent him, because I do not want any wrong impression to go abroad.

In reference to the item under discussion, could the minister tell the committee just what is the situation as between the renter and the landlord? That is to say, if the renter refuses to sign the landlord's application, does the whole amount of the bonus go to the renter, or does he merely receive his share based upon his share of the crop?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: Under the law as it has existed since early this session, if the renter refuses to sign the statement that the other man is his landlord, the money goes to the renter.

Just to keep the record straight, this is the note I received from the hon. member for Moose Jaw: "No. 1 northern yesterday $1.05J. Will bet you ten dollars it will close higher to-day." I think the hon1. member has some advance information on what is going to happen, or I would take him up.

There was a statement made by the minister which I think should not be allowed to go without someone taking exception to it. He pointed out that the farmer was in a position either to take his 90 cents advance now or to sell on the open market.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture

speechtext: If the chairman rules that I am not allowed to continue with this matter, I shall comply with his ruling; otherwise I should like to make a short statement.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I am in the hands of the committee, but we have been discussing items which were passed previously, and the minister had to answer some questions which

Supply-Agriculture
were put to him at that time. I do not believe we should go all over the items which have been passed.
I understand that, but I should like your ruling as to whether or not the statement I wish to make is in order.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I believe the committee would allow the hon. member to make a brief statement. We are on item 31, which provides for wheat acreage reduction payments and administration expenses in connection therewith. If the hon. member wants to make a brief statement in reply to the answer given by the minister, I believe it would be in order.

Thank you, Mr. Chairman. My statement will be brief. The farmer was not in a position either to deliver grain to the board and accept the ninety cents Fort William price, or to sell on the open market and take the SI .02 Fort William.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: It is the ninety cents advance, not price.

Yes, the ninety cents advance. Thousands of these farmers were in no position to take a chance on the ninety cents advance because no opportunity was given them to get hold of any cash last fall. They were allowed to deliver only five bushels to the acre, which was the opening quota. Since that time the quota has been raised, and the government have promised to take 280 million bushels of wheat from western Canada, but they have not taken that even yet. The farmer is in debt. He has not been allowed to sell a cash crop. What he sold did not cover the cost of harvesting, taxes and other indebtedness. He has had to sell what he could to get cash, and was forced to take the few cents extra he could get on the open market.
That is not correct.

The hon. member can make his statement when I am through. I say that is why the farmer was forced to sell his grain where he could get most cash. I do not know what the grain exchange does except to take the farmer's profit. The grain exchange is allowed to clean up on what might have been the farmer's profits. I believe that if you took the subsidies that have to be paid to agriculture and added them up you would get an amount about equal to the profits made by the grain exchange.

I should like to have an _ amplification of the statement made by the minister in answer to the hon. member for
Acadia. Do I understand that the owner of a piece of land who rents it cannot get the money to which he is entitled unless the renter is prepared to sign a certain form?
That is correct.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: Yes.

In my part of the country leases have been in effect for a number of years but because they were drawn up at a time when there was no crop bonus, no clause was put in to cover that. It seems an intolerable state of affairs that a man who rents the land that he owns should not be entitled to his fair share of the proceeds from working that land during the year. He is entitled to one-third share of the crop, and surely the man who owns the land and pays the taxes and looks after its upkeep is entitled to his share. I know cases where tenants, for reasons best known to themselves, have quarrelled with their landlord but have nevertheless stayed on the land, and under the law they can continue to stay there and do comparatively no work and take the proceeds of this wheat acreage bonus. I emphatically protest against that. Why not put ourselves in this position, that where a landlord produces a lease to the officials he shall be entitled to a share of the crop despite the fact that the tenant might be recalcitrant about signing any particular form submitted to him?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: The only reason we do not do it, so far as the administration is concerned, is that that is what the law says. We passed the law in this house at this session; the whole matter was then discussed, and the law was made as it has been recited. That is why the administration has to do things in this way.
Has the minister the wheat acreage reduction by provinces for 1943?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
There are no final
wheat acreage reduction figures for 1943. I have the wheat acreage reduction figures for Alberta for 1942.

I understood the
minister to say that the approximate reduction for 1943 would be ten million.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: The figures cannot be completed until the season is much more advanced. The final totals cannot be made up until about a year from now.
But the minister gave an approximate figure of ten million.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
That is only an estimate.
Supply-Agriculture
You have no figure for 1943?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: No actual final figures.

Somebody interjected when
I was speaking a while ago that I was acting for a mortgage company. May I point out that I have personal knowledge of many cases where the land is owned by private individuals, sometimes by widows with children. It does seem to me that consideration should be given to both sides of the case.
How many more applications for wheat acreage reduction bonus have there been this year than last year?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: We have not the figures for this year, but the number would be about the same.

I have a clipping here from the Regina Leader Post in which Mr. Gray, the director at Regina, says that there are
14,000	more applications this year, and I was wondering why there are more. Are there new people coming in?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
That would be new
people coming in. The 14,000 would be in addition, but as members of the committee know, the application for payment is not required to be made until after July 1. While a farmer might have given indication of his intention to apply earlier than that, he might afterwards change his mind and not reduce his acreage at all.

This clipping is dated
June 7.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: The regulations provide that the farmer is not required to make application for payment of the bonus until after July 1. He can make it at any time after that. He might state his intention to apply before the 30th of May, but with conditions as they have been, many people would probably change their intentions. When the applications come in for payment we shall be much more certain as to the number of farmers reducing their acreage than we could be simply by taking their indication of intention.

In view of the different
method of determining the wheat acreage reduction this year, can we not expect a reduction in the number of inspectors in western Canada?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
We have reduced the
number. As a matter of fact, there are no permanent inspectors at all on wheat acreage

reduction or on prairie farm assistance. There is simply a list of individuals whose services have been used from time to time. Some are called in for two or three weeks, some for a month, others for two or three months. This year there are fewer than in 1941.

To come back to the amendment which was passed this session providing that the tenant must sign an agreement acknowledging his landlord, I remember distinctly that it was passed one evening after the dinner recess, by no means with the unanimous consent of the committee. Very shortly after that amendment was passed I asked the minister when we were in the railway committee room if we could not have an amendment to rectify what I believe is a wrong. I think it is not too late to do that yet. Some people have been taking advantage of this provision in the past, and if we go on with the law as it is now, we are only inviting more trouble. An amendment would make administration easier. But administrative difficulties can be overcome, and I think an amendment should yet be made to rectify the wrong of which we have spoken in this committee.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I do not think that that question is in order. We are dealing with reduction of wheat acreage.
That is exactly what the question is in connection with-who shall receive the respective shares of the wheat acreage reduction bonus.

Would the minister inform the committee why these inspectors are changed around? The department does not allow one of its inspectors, who works only during the summer-fallow and crop season, to remain more than one or two years in the same municipality. We have had, I believe, three different inspectors in the last three years in the Wolseley municipality. I would have thought that when an inspector has become acquainted with the farmers and has got to know the acreage and that sort of thing, he would make a better job than a new man. When any claim is in dispute and a second inspection is required, they have always sent in an outsider-which may be all right.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
Of course there are
different reasons for moving inspectors. Sometimes one man is left in a community much longer than another man is left in a community. For example, generally speaking, under prairie farm assistance-and both these operations are carried on under the same inspectors-we do not think it is desirable to have a man inspect his own township. There

Supply-Agriculture
are obvious reasons for that. Quite often farmers who live in a township have large families in the same township, or family connections there or somewhere in the vicinity, and we would rather put these men in some other locality than have them accused of being partial to those people with whom they may be closely associated.
That is one reason. Then, we find that one inspector will be particularly efficient in inspecting a certain kind of crop; that is, he may be very efficient at estimating the yield while a crop is standing. That man of course would be used in places where that work is being done. Other men may be particularly efficient along other lines; and if we have to move a man from the place where he was in order to give him work somewhere else in which he is particularly efficient, then we have to move some other person into the area to cover the work he has been doing; the other person may be more competent to do that work than he is. That is, generally speaking, the way in which it works.
In reply to the hon. member for Melfort, it might be well if I put the number of inspectors on record. There were 57 inspectors and 32 supervisors at work in the three provinces on June 30. I believe there are 17 districts in Saskatchewan and one supervisor over each district. Alberta is divided into districts, with one supervisor over each district there, and Manitoba is the same. These 32 men are permanently employed; they work the twelve months through, but the 57 inspectors are men whom we call up to do inspection work when it has to be done, in the summer months, and they are employed only part time. There were 57 of these on June 30.
Has the minister information as to the total number employed say in October 1942?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: I am afraid there may be less in October than now.
There are certain seasons of the year when there are more of them?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
Yes, there are certain seasons when the number is much higher, but this depends on the year, the type of the year and the extent to which work was done earlier. Somebody said a moment ago that under the act as it now is the procedure is much simpler than it was before, the reason being that now we are only checking on how much land a man took out of wheat and whether he is doing something with the land he took out of wheat. We are not particular about what he is doing; we simply say that as long as he is farming in a reasonable way and as long as he
has taken the land out of wheat, we pay him $2 an acre. It is much simpler to administer that and it takes much less inspection than when we had to determine how many acres of barley and rye and summer-fallow and grass he had as compared with 1940. Now, so long as he can satisfy the administration that he has reduced his wheat acreage as compared with 1940 and is doing something with the land which is essential to the operation of the farm, he gets his $2. It will be seen from this that the figures with regard to inspection in past years would not give us very much information upon which to go this year.
Is it the intention of the minister to make an inspection of each farm again this year?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: On the wheat acreage reduction we are taking the word of municipal secretaries to a greater extent this year than was done last year.
I find that municipal inspectors who commenced their duties other years on August .1 are beginning their inspections this year on July 1. Why would that be?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: One reason is that in spite of the fact that the law does not require one to make a claim until after the first of July, the administration have been encouraging farmers to make these claims earlier. Many people have put their claims in, and the greater number of claims being in makes it possible to have the inspections at an earlier time, and we hope the payments will be out at an earlier time.

Summer-fallow does not have to be done until the first of August. Might there not be a great deal of repetition in inspections of that kind, or does it apply only in the case of the fall rye which they have to check by the first of July. I would think that in the case of wheat reduction, summer-fallow and so on, it might be necessary for other inspectors to follow up, and that would be a costly procedure.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: Of course the very fact, as stated a moment ago, that we are relying much more on municipal secretaries for reports of that kind would not necessitate, perhaps, a second inspection. We would get information as to whether that land is still black or whether it is growing a crop. If it is not growing wheat but something else, we pay the S2.

Will the minister say whether all last year's vote was taken up, and if it
Supply-Agriculture

was, how is it that the vote this year is so much more? Is there to be a supplementary estimate?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: There always has to be a supplementary estimate, and that will come in on the supplementaries. This vote, as is known, was made up months ago; it came down very early in the session, and it is only the administrative end of the work plus some demands which we know have to be met. The outside amount this year, we estimate, will run to about $26,000,000. The addition to this will be in the supplementaries.
It was all taken up last year?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
There is about $2,000,000
of a carry-over of what was estimated last year.

Rather than pay $4,-
265,000	to get farmers to go out of production, it would be a whole lot better to spend this money in fixing a parity price and getting more production of wheat and other food in this country. The United States is encouraging the growth of food. At the Hot Springs food conference, which was held recently, in which forty-four countries participated, it was pointed out that there never was sufficient food in the world for all the people. I think we are going at this in the wrong way. The paying of a bonus in this form is, I think, entirely wrong, and probably in a few years' time we shall be working in the opposite direction. However, seeing this is the policy of the government in power I suppose we have to carry on with it.
There are two complaints under this policy which have come to my attention. One is that many of the farmers who have made applications found that there was no record of their applications having been received. When they stated "I went down and made my application," they were asked "When did you do it?" "Oh, on a certain date." "Well," was the reply, "we have no record in the office here." That farmer gets no redress. Is something being done to see that the farmer when he makes application receives a duplicate of the application form signed by the municipal secretary?
Another point is this. A number of farmers' found that they were too late putting in their application. The)' said they did not know they were supposed to have it in by a certain date. Is something being done to get in contact with the municipal councils in order that the councillors may inform everyone in their division that they must have their application in by the date specified?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
There are approximately
184.000	farmers paid under wheat acreage reduction, and I believe, speaking from memory, that the number that claimed they had made application or were entitled to make application in the first year, which of course would be the year in which there would be the greatest number of people who would not be informed, was six or seven hundred. There were 600 or 700 in that year who had to be considered afterwards, some of whom were allowed to collect. That is to say, we found that they had actually made application but their letters had either been misplaced or had not reached the proper authority. There are probably between
2.000	and 3,000 in addition to the 184,000 who actually did claim payment on wheat reduction but we did not consider that they properly came under the act, and there would be in addition to that, a few hundred who would come back and say that they did apply and the secretary of the municipality thought he had sent in the application. In those cases we check back and if we find the statement is correct the payment is made. There are cases where we are not satisfied with the man's statement and we say to such people that we have spent thousands of dollars putting this over the radio and in the local press and making statements about it generally so as to get it out to everyone we could possibly get in contact with by these means, and we have therefore to assume that these particular people had the same chance as everyone else. If therefore they did not apply until months afterwards we do not find it advisable to make these payments, and some have not been made. But there are very few compared with the total number.
Are there any exceptions to the rule with regard to those who do not apply on time?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: No; there are no exceptions, unless they can show that they did apply. There must be someone somewhere to prove that they made application.
If it is a matter of negligence on their part-

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: If we are satisfied that it is negligence on their part we do not pay anything.
Suppose the farmer claims that application was made and that the application was lost; do you accept his affidavit?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
It has to be supported by some other person. Someone has to know that he did make application. We do not accept his sworn statement by itself.

Supply-Agriculture

I have in mind a case which depends on this very point. This man claims that he did make applies tion but they have no record of it. He claims further that he consulted the secretary of the municipality but the secretary says that he does not recall it. The whole thing boils down to the question whether the department accepts the farmer's word or his sworn affidavit or whether it discards that type of proof.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: We will discuss the matter with him until we are satisfied one way or the other. I have some recollection of a case brought up by the member for Bow River, and I do not believe it is finally closed. As long as the man has any chance of giving proof that he did apply we will continue to try to find that proof.
But this is a brand new case.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: Oh; if it is a new one he is starting pretty late.
The minister says that there must be some independent support. If a neighbour supports the man's declaration and states that he knows he made application, is that accepted?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
I should not like to make a decision out of court. He will have to appear before someone and prove his statement, and if he proves it to the satisfaction of the officials he wTill be paid. If he does not, he will write to me and I shall have to go to the officials and see whether he made the mistake or they did. I get these letters from time to time.
One point was raised by the member for Yorkton which I cannot allow to pass without comment. He said that we are spending
34,000,000 to reduce production. That is not correct. We are spending 34,000,000 and some odd thousands to get more production of something we want, and that production will give greater returns than the production of wheat will yield. We are asking men to transfer from the production of *wheat, of which we have 650,000,000 bushels in store, to the production of something else which we can sell right away, and to do that we are asking them to transfer certain acreages from wheat over to other grain and grasses. That is not reducing production. That policy so far has resulted in greater returns from the farms than could have been obtained in any other way, both in quantity of food and in return in cash, and for that reason I do not want to allow that statement to pass.

I think the minister could save a good deal in this inspection work. In the first place, we have far too many inspectors. The municipalities have to do a great deal of this work. In making applications for this bonus the municipalities take nearly all applications and send them in and they have to get out a lot of information on the matter. They do a good deal of work apart from a certain portion of the actual inspection work. As I say, a good deal could be saved. The minister may not have the information before him at the moment, but will he take this as an order for return, so to speak, and give us the number of inspectors in Saskatchewan, their salaries and expense accounts for the last year, and at the same time the number of those men employed again this year. I should like to have that information on Hansard.
The minister said something about the efficiency of the inspectors. I may point out the efficiency of one or two of them. I was north of Moosomin last year sitting with a farmer in his yard when one of the inspectors drove in, in a car, in a hurry, and stepped out of the car and rapped at the door. He asked whether this farmer was Mr. so and so, and was told that he was. I had never met this man before, but he did not impress me with his manner. He drove in in a blustering sort of way. The farmer asked him if he would like to meet Mr. Perley and he said, "Sure." The farmer said, "This is Mr. Perley." We got into a discussion about inspection work and he told me that he could inspect any field of grain in that municipality on the fly. I questioned him about how careful he was in going through the fields and he said he did not have to do that. If he could not inspect any field of grain, to get the information he required, by just driving past in a car he would not be on that job.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: That would be right this year on wheat acreage reduction.

It did not happen to be right last year. We were looking at that crop from the barn and I was not impressed by that fellow. There were many complaints in that district regarding the manner in which he did his work, and he received a salary for it.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
A return was brought down on February 20, 1943, giving all the information up to that date. Let me say again that it will be absolutely impossible to give a return right up to date. In the first place I would have to send to the office in Regina, and they would be able to give it
Supply-Agriculture

only up to about a month ago. I could not possibly get that while the session is on, up to date.
Could the minister give the number of men on the job this year?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: There are only 57 on the job, up to date, although last year before the end of the season the number reached about 400 who had been on at some time or another.
There should not be so many required this year.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: No.
The statement of the minister was partly true.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: It was all true.

I think the records will show, however, that the increased summer-fallow in the last few years has brought about a reduction in the possible production of food. We do not have what we could have had in the way of production. We have taken
10.000.000 acres out of the production of wheat, and only part of that has been put into coarse grains. The minister's own statement was that a few years ago we had too much wheat. Well, if he wishes to get production he will have to give the farmer a parity price. If he does that he will get the production he wants. The farmer does not want the bonus if he can get parity price.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: We have got more food now than we ever got at any other price.

Because you also got rain, which you may not get this year. I have a further question: Are duplicate copies of farmers' applications to be given to them this year, so that they will have evidence that they have made application?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: When I got mine I got three copies, only two of which had to be returned. I was permitted to keep one. I presume every other farmer will get the same.

Has that been the procedure in the past?
M,r. GARDINER: Yes, that is the procedure.
Has it been in the past?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
Not always in the past, perhaps. We did start at some time to do
it, and we are still doing it.

The farmer is entitled to a copy of his application if he wishes to
[Mr. Gardinpr.J
have it. Something has been said about municipal officials doing a great deal of this work. I know in my own province this work is heavy. Many of the farmers look upon their municipal offices as their community centre. They go to the clerk and find out a great many things which otherwise it would be very difficult for the farmer to learn. I suppose the municipal clerk is allowed something for taking these applications. I do not know whether he is allowed enough, but I trust that the minister, so long as this scheme is in operation, will continue to work through the municipal offices in the prairie provinces, because certainly they are of very great assistance to the farmers, generally speaking. Otherwise the farmers would be in a quandary, completely, if they had to write to the head offices, or chase up an inspector. I appreciate the work that has been done by municipal officials in those offices, and I presume the same has been done throughout all the prairie provinces. I trust it may be continued, and that they will receive appropriate remuneration for the work they are doing.

I understood the minister's statement to be that the purpose of the wheat acreage reduction bonus is not that of reducing the yield, but rather to increase coarse grain production. As the minister will know, in parts of Alberta, and I believe in some of Saskatchewan, there has been serious drought. In some instances wheat which was sowed never came up. That ground is now being cultivated, and it may possibly be sown to oats. However, if it is not sown to oats it will be summer-fallowed, thereby increasing the production next year. Will there be a wheat acreage reduction bonus on that land?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: No. It is the action taken, not the weather, which controls the payment under wheat acreage reduction. Under the Prairie Farm Assistance Act. if it goes into operation, assistance would be given to persons w*ho are dried out during the season. But so far as this act is concerned, it relates to a man's action. That is why these inspectors are sent out-to find out whether the farmer has done differently. If we find that a man had sown wheat in the spring and ploughed it up in June, he would not be counted for wheat acreage reduction. It may be that some would get awray with it, but that is not the intention.

For the good of the country as a whole would it not be better to change that arrangement? If the farmer leaves that grain as it is, and does not touch it, he will have a chance of getting $2 an acre prairie farm assistance bonus, but the country will

Supply-Agriculture
ttot get anything from it. The country is losing production by this procedure. It would be far better for Canada if that farmer were to cultivate that land and put in coarse grains this year. But if he is not going to be eligible for wheat acreage reduction bonus he may think, "Well, if I leave it as it is I can get $2 an acre prairie farm assistance bonus for it, so I will leave it." I think it would be well if the minister were to consider that, and make it possible for the farmer to get the benefit of this provision.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: I am pleased to see that the hon. member for Acadia is a much better farmer than the hon. member for Yorkton. It would seem that the hon. member for Yorkton thinks that by putting land under summer-fallow we reduce production. Every farmer in the committee must know that during difficult years the farmers were cropping more of their land than they should have been cropping under good farming practice, in the hope of getting a good crop some year to pay off some of their bills. We all know now that we were mistaken in that. And we know it more than for any other reason because of the acreages summer-fallowed under this act. We have grown more grain on the same acreage, even*-with as little rainfall as we have had in other years, in 1942 than we ever grew before. And one of the reasons was the increased summer-fallow. On my own farm I have convinced myself that I am going to summer-fallow more land than I did in the past. I have been convinced that, if I do, I will grow more bushels over any twenty-year period than I ever grew before, and I think most farmers in western Canada have been convinced of the same thing. Increasing summer-fallow until you reach fifty per cent of your land-anywhere between twenty-five per cent and fifty per cent-does not necessarily reduce production.
Are they doing it this year?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: They are not anywhere near fifty per cent. They could still increase their summer-fallow and farm to better advantage over a period of years. I am pointing out that it is wrong to say that an increase in summer-fallow cuts down production. The fact is that you are not cutting down production; rather you are increasing it.

I do not know anything about summer-fallow, when compared with the minister; certainly he knows more about it than I do. But I should like to ask two questions arising out of his controversy with the hon. member for Yorkton. The minister introduced a policy of wheat
acreage reduction, and paid a bonus to western farmers for not growing wheat, on the theory that if the farmer did not grow wheat he would grow coarse grain. He believed that in that way he would have a production of a greater variety of grain. The minister and his officials believed that that would be more beneficial for the country generally. I am inclined to think that the policy had that effect. But what I wish to know, and what the farmers of eastern Canada are asking, is why this policy has not been made available to other parts of Canada, if indeed it is a sound policy.
The second question I would ask is this: why was it not considered good husbandry and good economy for the government to indicate to farmers that they should grow less wheat and more coarse grains, and not pay them for doing it-for doing something which a good farmer ought to do in his own interest? We had the same problem in a very much smaller degree in New Brunswick. The farmers there desired to raise seed potatoes. If they followed their own bent they would all be growing seed potatoes, and some of them would not even have a cow. That has happened in some parts of Maine. But they were all shown in years gone by that that does not pay. Those of us who had an interest in agriculture-and I do not mean that we all got down to the dirt and dug with them-have for many years been trying to preach to the farmers of the Saint John river valley and in the northern part of New Brunswick, that they should not put all their eggs in one basket. But nobody ever suggested that the farmers of New Brunswick- the farmers in Carleton county or Victoria county-should be paid for not raising potatoes. They do not understand why western farmers are paid a bonus for reducing their wheat acreage, while the farmers in New Brunswick get nothing. That is something the minister must explain to the farmers in my part of the country before the next election.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: I can explain it now.

I wish
the minister would explain why that economy is practised in western Canada, and the rest of Canada has to foot the bill and get nothing out of it. I want to know that.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
In the first place I
would say that while the hon. member's statement will be looked upon by farmers in other parts of Canada as being very accurate, I do not think it is exactly accurate. For example we induced farmers in western Canada to grow feed grain, not only to feed their own live
Supply-Agriculture

stock but to feed live stock in eastern Canada and in the United States. In order to provide assistance to the eastern farmer, we put a ceiling on the price that he had to pay for this feed grain, though we did not put a ceiling on the price to the American farmer. In addition we paid the freight from Fort William to the destination in the east.

That is
the form of bonus the eastern farmer gets.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
Yes; we are giving him the grain at the price realized by the western farmer, plus the freight as far as Fort William. Last year the assistance which was given to the eastern farmers on that basis amounted to something like $10,000,000. In the coming year the assistance given to western farmers under war acreage reduction will amount to about $26,000,000. It may be said that the amount paid to do the job in the east is less than half the amount being paid to do the other job in the west, but to the amount expended in the east in this connection must be added the money we have paid for fertilizer, assistance which we are not paying on the prairies. We are assisting with fertilizer to the extent that we can get it, though we have not been paying for it in connection with potatoes. Until a few weeks ago we thought there would be enough potatoes, and that there would not be a market for all of them. Now we find that there will be a market and that we cannot get enough, but whether or not that will be the case next year I cannot say. However, we do try to keep that balance.
The hon. member asked why we should pay the farmer who is a wheat grower. We do so for the same reason that we pay the Nova Scotia apple grower. The wheat grower could not market all his grain after the early stages of the war and therefore would not rave been able to stay on the land if some-hing had not been done for him. So far is the apple grower is concerned, he does not get the full amount of the assistance provided. It works out at the rate of something like $400 or $500 per family that we have had to pay in one year. It is true that there are only between four and five thousand families, but the amount we have paid in order to keep the apple industry going in Nova Scotia, and to a limited extent outside that province, amounts to about the figure I have mentioned per family. We have never paid that much per family in western Canada, but I submit that is no reason why we should not pay the amount we are paying in connection with apples. As I have said, it does not all go to the apple grower; his is a different line

of activity, and you must take into consideration the man who puts in the fertilizer, the man who puts in the spray, the cost of the barrels, and all that sort of thing. However, that is what it is costing us. The total is much smaller because we are dealing only with about four thousand families. When you have to deal with 250,000 or 280,000 families the amount piles up, but the individual farmer does not get any more.
In reply to the last question, the wheat growers have said to us, as the hon. member for Qu'Appelle has just finished saying, "We cannot produce wheat at less than SI a bushel." We have replied, "Well, you cannot produce wheat even at $1 a bushel if, as a result of weather conditions, you do not grow any wheat." So we provided those farmers with prairie farm assistance in order to keep them on the land during periods of that kind in order that they might produce another crop the next year. Then the war came along, and after the fall of France we found that our markets on the continent had gone and there was no possibility of marketing much of our wheat. Every organization in western Canada-and I say this for the benefit of the , hon. member for Yorkton-came here, led by the wheat pools, and asked us to quota the deliveries of wheat. The figure of 280,000,000 bushels is the figure of the delegation of four hundred that came here in the spring of 1942. I pleaded with them over in the hotel to ask for 300,000,000 bushels, but the best I could get out of them was to ask the government for not less than 280,000,000 bushels. If I had been the treasurer I would have done just what the present treasurer did; I would have said, "Since they mention not less than 280,000,000 bushels, why make it more?" I sat right on the platform with all the pool officials and the four hundred delegates, with the Minister of Finance, the Minister of Mines and Resources and the Minister of Trade and Commerce. I said, "I have asked the government to put that figure at
300,000,000 bushels," but even after that when they came in with their recommendation it asked for from 280,000.000 to 300,000,000 bushels.
I just make that statement in order to place the facts before hon. members and to show that the quota was not fixed by the government alone; that this was the reasonable way to deal with it, as worked out by the grain handling companies together with the farm organizations and presented to the government to assure that all farmers would get some return. As a result we have placed the marketing of wheat under quota. I believe every farmer in western Canada will

Supply-Agriculture
say that under the quota he has had the most orderly marketing of wheat in the history of the marketing of grain in western Canada; but because we were not able to take all the wheat and were not able to pay the advance which farmers thought they ought to have we said, "Now, we want you to take some of this land out of wheat. The only cash crop you have in sight is wheat. We are not going to increase the advance beyond ninety cents, but we will give you an acreage payment on the land you take out of wheat and put into some other production, because we want that other production." We gave them the money because we felt that otherwise, not being able to market their full crop of wheat, they would not be able to continue to produce. So wTe gave them acreage payments which one year amounted to almost $35,000,000, which last year came to $21,000,000 and which this year we estimate will amount to $26,000,000. We are giving that assistance to farmers who produced wheat before the war, when they had a market for it, in order that they may remain in the production of wheat to a sufficient extent to be able to swing back into wheat, if they should be required to do so, or to go on producing live stock. We hope the future may be such that we can remain in live stock production without hurting people in other parts of Canada; but if in order to assist agriculture right across t'he country it becomes necessary for 'the west to go back into wheat, to supply some demand somewhere in the world, I*am sure it will be to the advantage of those in the east for us to go back into the production of wheat. At the moment, however, we do not think that should be done.

The minister made one statement which I cannot allow to go unchallenged, to the effect that the assistance given in connection with freight, amounting to about $10,000,000, all went to the benefit of the eastern farmer. I cannot agree with that statement, for the reason that if that freight assistance had not been given, the western farmer would have had to take lower prices for his coarse grains; otherwise the eastern farmer could not have used them. The farmer of the east could not pay that additional cost and continue to produce beef, dairy products or hogs. Therefore if this assistance had not been given, that grain would not have been used in the east and the farmers of the west would have been forced to sell at lower prices.

I listened to the minister's explanation, and he certainly made a reasoned argument. At the same
time, after listening to agricultural debates in this house for a good many years, I wonder if the western farmer would not prefer a decent price for his wheat instead of bonuses. I think that is the issue. From an economic standpoint I cannot understand a member of a Liberal government advocating bonuses. I recall a pamphlet I saw in 1935, I think put out by 'the present Minister of Agriculture, which stated, "Dollar wheat will pay your debts. Dollar wheat will pay your taxes." That pamphlet did the trick in Saskatchewan.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: We got it.
I agree; it was a smart trick on the people of Saskatchewan, but they never got dollar wheat.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: Oh, yes; we got $1.50 wheat after that and have dollar wheat now.

You got the votes, too. However, I did not rise to make a political speech. I should like the minister to answer one further question before one o'clock. Is this to be a permanent policy? Are we to look forward to government bonuses, not only for the duration of the war, when quotas are being set and markets have been lo^t, but as a permanent thing?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: I think I said the first year wTe hoped it would be only for one year. For that reason we did not put it in the form of legislation.
