We have now gone into the third year and we certainly hope that it will not be necessary to have this continued after the war, but there are grave doubts of our being able to do other than what we are doing in some form while the war is on unless before the end of the war there is a very decided increase in the market for wheat. I want it to be quite clear the record of the meeting of the 400 farmers who came to Ottawa is there to be read; every word that was said was taken down; there was evidenced a decided determination that the acreage payments we were making should not be an alternative for dollar wheat. The farmers were more prepared to accept 90 cent wheat plus these payments than they were to have dollar wheat without them. They believed that it gave some insurance. During the discussion this definite question was asked: If we get dollar wheat, does it mean the taking away of these acreage payments? I had to get up and say that as long as I was Minister of Agriculture the prairie farm assistance payments were going to stay.

That is a permanent government policy; that answers my question.
Supply-Agriculture

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: The prairie farm assistance was in effect before the war and is permanent policy.
That was because of the drought.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: They wanted the acreage payments as well as whatever advance was made on wheat.

I think it should be made clear that the statement made by the minister was in connection with the prairie farm assistance bonus but did not refer to wheat acreage reduction bonus.
At one o'clock the committee took recess.
The committee resumed at three o'clock.

There is one observation that ought to be made before this item carries. It does not bear exactly on the topic under consideration, but inasmuch as the minister told us at the beginning of his remarks that one of his chief concerns now was to find a way of storing the crop that is coming in, I think it would be well to spend a moment or two on this question.
I suggest to the minister that the only really thoroughly satisfactory long-range way of dealing with the storage of grain is to provide for storage on the farm. That will require a reversal of policy to a considerable degree and necessitate a great deal of government credit being advanced to farmers to enable them to build granaries to store the grain. But I believe it will be found to be the correct method of approach in the long run. There are several reasons why.
If the farmers were enabled to store grain in granaries which they themselves built and filled, and were to hold the grain in trust for the Dominion of Canada, having received payment for it and being paid storage regularly on it at very much the same rate as is being paid to the elevators, then in due time the farmers would come to possess the grain, or at least they would possess the granaries. The farmer would be required to keep the grain in good condition, and to show sufficient evidence to satisfy the inspector that he had done so before he would be permitted to market his new quota of grain. I believe this device would render the government secure against the loss of the grain, which would then be held for the government and be just as readily available to the government as though it were stored at a terminal elevator.
There are two or three reasons why this would ultimately lead to a satisfactory state of

affairs. In times of drought, when grain has had to be shipped out to farmers for feed or seed, a good deal of expense has been entailed which would not have been necessary had the grain been stored on the farm and consequently been in the community where it was later to be used.
There is another serious aspect of the question. We may have disorder in this country at some time. We are so accustomed to looking upon our country as being secure from all internal commotion that we are likely to find it impossible to project ourselves into a state of affairs where there might be disorder, and if such occurred in the future it would be greatly to our advantage if we had the grain stored out on the farm where it would be much more readily accessible to the people than if it had to be distributed out from large terminal elevators.
The question will be raised immediately, where will the material be obtained now with which to construct these granaries? It is my settled conviction, from such information as has been given me, that there are a good many places in Canada where lumber of a more or less low grade could be manufactured were it not for the restrictions imposed on the manufacturer as a result of the activities of the timber controller. If the Minister of Agriculture were to take this matter up really seriously with the Minister of Munitions and Supply and the other ministers concerned, I believe a way could be found of rendering available a considerable quantity of lumber which is not now going into the hands of those who could use it.
May I suggest also that there is a good deal of cement which could be used to a considerable extent in the construction of granaries on the farm. Certainly it would be better to store the grain in that way than to allow it to accumulate in great piles on the ground, filling with anxiety the minister and everybody else concerned.
To sum up, may I suggest to the minister that a good deal of care and attention should be given to the matter of enabling us to store our grain on the farm.

There is one phase of this
question which should be discussed at some time, and that is the question of advances to the farmers on the grain they have stored on their farms. While the committee was sitting this morning, I got a letter in the mail box from a man who had been served thirty days' notice to get off his farm. He has feed and he has a number of brood sows and hogs, but he cannot sell the grain that he has, and he has been asked to get off the place. I

Supply-A cjricul ture
[DOT]understand that he happens to be in a fairly good financial condition. This is only one *case of which I have knowledge, but I think that some interest should be taken in this phase of the question under discussion.

I should like to revert to
the question I asked this morning with respect to paying the bonus on burnt-out land which is now being cultivated. Would these men be eligible for the prairie farm assistance bonus?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture

A few years ago they were told that they would have to leave the land

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture

There is no regulation

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
All I can say is that
we do pay a premium on cheese. If it grades 93 the premium is one cent; if it grades 94 the premium is two cents. I know of no provision in the legislation or the regulations that
would prevent a man who is producing high-grade cheese in some small plant of his own on his farm from getting the premium if the cheese is of the proper quality.
His trouble is to get it graded.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: It has to be cheddar cheese.
He is making a cheddar cheese, but cannot get it graded.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: I do not think that that should put him in a position where he cannot get the premium. I think we ought to provide for its being graded. I have not in mind the details of the case. It is somewhere in the northern part of the province, is it not?
That is right.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: Then probably there is only one man doing this. Probably the only way we could have a check made would be to get someone at the agricultural college at Saskatoon to go and make the check. I do not think this man should be deprived of his premium because someone is not coming around regularly and checking it up.
The minister's opinion is different from the opinion I got from the department before.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: This is the view that I express. I will try to bring my view to bear on the department.

I ask the minister to break this item down into two parts. One part I believe is devoted to a premium of one cent and two cents on high grade cheese; the other is for improvements to cheese factories. I should like to know how much money was expended last year under each item, and what is anticipated will be spent this year.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: The amount has been $350,000 for the construction and $1,600,000 for premiums. There is some difficulty at present in getting priorities for equipment, and we do not estimate that more than about $275,000 will be utilized for equipment; the remainder will be required for premium.

I suppose if this amount has been expended from year to year for the last three or four years since the Cheese Factory Improvement Act came into force, by this time most of the factories are properly equipped, though no doubt there are some which are not. However, I did not intend to emphasize that part of it. What improvement

Supply-Agriculture

has been made in cheese production since the bonus has been in existence? Are we getting a larger percentage of our cheese to grade No. 1 and No. 2 than we did formerly, and if so, to what extent? Perhaps the minister also would say something more about our cheese exports to the old country. Is it likely that we shall be able to fill our quota this year? Evidently up to the present our cheese production for this year is far behind what it was last year.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: As has been stated on a number of occasions, we had a higher production of cheese last year than we have had since very early in the century, and some of that increased production was due to the fact that we encouraged the production of cheese in the winter months. Starting with January and down to April there was a very great increase of the production of cheese as compared with the preceding years. If one takes the whole year into consideration, the quality is down in 1942 as compared with 1941. If one takes just the summer season when the better cheese was being made in all preceding years the position is about the same. Even in spite of the fact that we have had a great increase of production the position is about the same. To give the exact percentage of first-grade cheese to all cheese produced : in 1939 we had 91-72 per cent; 1940, 94-54 per cent; 1941, 95-51 per cent. There was a constant increase up to that time. In 1942, with 93-68 per cent, it is down as compared with 1941, but one has to make allowance for the two things I mentioned, the much greater production, and the fact that we produced so much in the winter months.
Do we ship that lower grade cheese to the old1 country?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: As long as it is No. 1, 2 or 3 it may be shipped to Britain, but if a larger proportion of it in the winter is not in those grades, not so large a portion of it goes to Great Britain. As a matter of fact we did encourage the increase in the winter time in 1942 to supply local markets.
Has there been any application for assistance under this item to cheese factories in western Canada, and are there any inspectors there to inspect cheese for the purpose of the bonus?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
Most of the inspectors, of course, are in Ontario and Quebec, because that is where most of the cheese factories are, but there are some in the other provinces. The numbers of factories, with the amounts

paid, are these: New Brunswick, two, amount paid $113.33; Prince Edward Island, two. $252.75; Quebec, original 143. supplementary 80, total subsidies $189,221.50; Ontario, original 67, supplementary 16; total subsidies $28,922.93; Alberta, two, $2,032.43; British Columbia, one, S9S1.85. There have been no applications from Manitoba and Saskatchewan?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: I do not think there were any in 1942, but my recollection is that there was one in Manitoba one or two years earlier. I doubt if there were any from Saskatchewan. We make very little cheese.

Is there any collaboration between the Department of Agriculture and the Department of Munitions and Supply as to priorities for cheese makers in respect to gasoline and tires? I think the question, although not strictly the minister's responsibility, is of interest.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: We have a man, Mr. Armstrong, who is working all the time in connection with all these priorities, and he takes up with the officials of the Department of Munitions and Supply any complaints which are brought to our attention. On quite a number of occasions we have secured assistance for the people concerned, but there are many cases for which it is impossible to get priority.

This forenoon we discussed
the question of transportation of grain from the west to the east, and I understood that the reason given why more grain is not transported is lack of railway facilities. I have just had the pleasure of listening to the distinguished president of the Canadian National Railways with his officials. He stated that actually they could carry more grain than is offdred. I thought it well to bring that to the attention of the minister so that the farmers of Quebec may be allowed to have more grain to help them in raising their stock.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
I cannot let that statement pass without correction. I do not know what the officials said in the committee, but I have sat in committees and tried to arrange with the railways for some considerable time to provide cars. The railways have done

their best, but there is no one moving grain in Canada to the extent that we want it moved, neither the railways nor anyone else. We are not blaming anyone for that. subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: The house resumed from Wednesday, July 7, consideration in committee of a resolution to grant to his majesty certain sums of money for the carrying out of measures consequent upon the existence of a state of war-Mr. Usley-Mr. Bradette in the chair.

speakerposition: topic
stagedirection
speechtext: Hon. J.t L. ILSLEY (Minister of Finance): I think we had better finish the wartime prices and trade board items. One item has been carried, the wartime prices and trade board proper, but the allied agencies have not been dealt with. I think they should all be dealt with at the same time. The next item is the Commodity Prices Stabilization Corporation, and then follow two crown companies. It would interrupt the sequence badly if we were to vary that order.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: What item does the minister wish to have called now?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The Commodity Prices
Stabilization Corporation, $120,000,000.

I sat in the house all yesterday and I wished to ask a certain question, but the relevant item was passed in my absence. I understood that No. 1 would not be finished. I left at ten minutes to-eleven. There is one matter to which I should like to make reference if I may.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I cannot take any exception to that, because I said last night that there were certain questions unanswered which I thought I could answer on the next item without any undue stretching of the rules.

War Appropriation-Prices Stabilization

What I have to say refers to a matter which I know will receive the approval of hon. members generally. It is something that is being advanced not by way of criticism but from a desire to rivet the attention of the house and the country on the necessity of assuring men who were in business and who come back from overseas of the opportunity of securing a permit to carry on business. I am going to give a concrete example which has just come to hand. It reveals I submit a serious situation when the rehabilitation of the men who have served overseas and who return is being considered. Since November 2, 1942, no new business may be opened up within designated lines of business, and the result is that service men who were formerly engaged in business, say, in a retail store, which is the only training they have had, when they come back are denied the opportunity of carrying on that business. It is the only business they know anything about, and their experience fits them for nothing else. The instance I have in mind is sufficiently definite to be regarded as typical of the result of a strict application of the regulations. This ex-soldier, William W. McIntosh, served overseas twenty-five months. He had been running a hardware store in Vonda in Saskatchewan before he enlisted in September, 1939. He has two sons, and both of those boys are overseas. He left his business under the control of a relative who did [DOT]not operate it any too well, and finally, in August 1941, the relative closed the business, there being a large amount of hardware still on hand. Finally this man returned from overseas. For thirty-five years he and his father before him had operated this hardware store. There had always been two hardware stores in the town. When he was discharged from the army the only place he could go was back to the operation of the business, in respect of which he still had a large amount of stock on hand. On April 27, he wrote the wartime prices and trade board setting out the facts I have given to the house, and also stating that in order to establish himself in civilian life it would be necessary for him to open his store, that being his only means of support. In his letter he stated further:
, There is a good stock on hand, many articles which are unobtainable in the market to-day. It will not be necessary for me to purchase a great deal of stock except for replacement of goods which I may sell from the present stock.
He was discharged in March, and wrote this letter in April. He received no reply, and again on May 20 he wrote the wartime prices and trade board at Saskatoon advising them that on April 27 last he had made an application to the board for a permit to reopen his
(Mr. Ilsley]
business, after being discharged from the Canadian active service army. Then he said in his letter:
I have as yet received no word as to whether or not my application was received or whether it was granted or refused. Surely some decision must have been arrived at after a period of over three weeks.
On May 27 he received a letter from Mr. J. E. Housey, the representative in Saskatoon, acknowledging receipt of the letter of May 20, and stating:
We would also like to know if anyone else has started in this business in the town of Vonda. If so, your store would have to be treated as a new entrant into business.
No store had been opened in the interval, and he so replied, stating further in his letter:
I would say that no one else has started in a hardware business in the town of Vonda since the closing of my store, and my store cannot be considered a new entrant. It is now over a month since I made application for a permit. In view of the fact that my small capital is being depleted for living expenses and I have no other income until I can open my business and reestablish myself in civil life, I would ask you to rush this matter through as quickly as you possibly can.
On May 31 Mr. Housey wrote again, stating:
Owing to the fact that this store has been closed since August, 1941, it will have to be considered as a new entrant into business, as order 184 states that a business not operated or closed for a year prior to November 2, 1942, must be considered a new entrant into business.
Nothing further was done, and on June 15 one of the wartime prices and trade board representatives at Regina, Mrs. May W. Neal, wrote to him as follows:
Will you be good enough to inform us what other stores in your community are handling the same lines of hardware, and if there are no others how close the nearest hardware stores are located to you. We must also know the definite date on which your business was temporarily suspended.
The soldier replied on June 16. In part he wrote:-
When I was discharged from the army I had a limited amount of capital but this is rapidly being used up in living costs while awaiting permit to open my store. It appears to me, that in my case, where I had served three and a half years in the active service army and over two years in England, that my application could have been granted immediately and every assistance given to me to reestablish myself in civilian life without assistance from the government.
As the matter now stands I will very shortly either have to open my business or apply to the government for assistance, as I cannot go on living without some means of supporting myself.

War Appropriation-Prices Stabilization
He received no reply to that letter. Then he wrote again on June 27 to the wartime prices and trade board, stating:
I cannot understand why it should take two months to deal with my application.
He received no reply to that, and, finally, on July 5, he wrote a letter which is undoubtedly the culmination of over two and a half months of delay. In that letter he said:
It will be ten weeks ago to-morrow since I made my application for a permit from your board. Repeated requests for some action one way or another have had no results and I have been put to considerable expense and monetary loss through this unnecessary and unwarranted delay.
Then he states something which I believe I should place before the committee. These are his words:
I can no longer support myself without some means of subsistence, and if no permit is received from your board by next Monday, July 12, my store will be open for business without a permit.
That part of the letter I do not try to justify. But here was a man who served his country, and whose two sons are overseas. He has engaged in .only one business, namely, the hardware business. I know I will receive the sympathetic cooperation both of the Minister of Finance and the Minister of Pensions and National Health, and also that of hon. members generally, when I ask that this rule which prevents the opening of a business be not applied against men returning from overseas. When a man returns from overseas, and wishes to reengage in business in the town in which he formerly operated, he should be given an opportunity to do so in order to rehabilitate himself. Otherwise the observance of the letter of the regulation issued by the wartime prices and trade board means that our men, after they have served their country, are going to be denied the opportunity of rehabilitating themselves. I believe an undertaking along that line would do much to improve the morale of the men who serve.
Practically every able-bodied man in this little town of Vonda is in the army-people of various races, including besides people of British origin, French, Ukrainian and German. When these people see the regulations strictly enforced against a man who returns from overseas, thereby denying him the opportunity of earning a livelihood, it does not make for the type of feeling which should exist. I would ask the minister to alter the letter of the law, so far as the opening of new businesses is concerned, in respect of men who go overseas. When they return, they
ask for and have the right to demand the opportunity to earn a livelihood. I believe all hon. members agree that these men should receive everything the country can give them fairly, and surely they should not be denied the right to earn a livelihood in the business in which they were formerly engaged.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
This is the first I have
known of the facts, although I understand my hon. friend communicated them to my parliamentary assistant this morning. On the recital of the facts I cannot, of course, justify the delay in dealing with the case. I do not know if there is any explanation for the delay, but I shall have the case investigated. The hon. gentleman asks me to give an undertaking that a principle will be established that men returning from overseas will be exempt from the provisions of the order preventing the establishment of new businesses.
If they were previously engaged in business, or if their training in civil life was in business.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I very much doubt if permits are denied now in cases of that kind. There has been delay in the case mentioned, I admit; but I just want to point out that this order preventing persons from going into business is of course a serious interference with the freedom of the individual, perhaps one of the most serious of the interferences that have been set up by the government. It was set up because, as persons in business understand full well, in a great many lines the stocks that are given to one trader are virtually taken away from other traders, and the order was passed for the protection of retailers and persons now engaged in business of that kind. I do not think the hon. gentleman would advocate the rescission of that rule; I do not know whether he would or not.

I do not argue
the abolition of the rule, but I do argue against its application to discharged soldiers; otherwise you are going to deny men who have served overseas an opportunity to rehabilitate themselves.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
My colleague the Minister
of Pensions and National Health has made representations with regard to these men returning from overseas. He has submitted that they should be granted permits; the matter has been fully discussed, and he has just handed me this memorandum: "Gordon said he would make reasonable allowance for men setting up in business after discharge by allowing quotas of rationed goods on special basis. The man's difficulty was that he had no quota," this was a British Columbia case,
4508	COMMONS
War Appropriation-Prices Stabilization
"not having been in business during the basic period." I do not know just what that means, but I know that special consideration is given to cases of returned soldiers. In view of what the hon. gentleman has said; in view of the fact that this man had a store, I should think this would be a case in which special consideration would be given, but there are cases in which men want to buy stores and reestablish themselves in that way.
They want to start new businesses.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes. If that were allowed generally-perhaps it is allowed generally; I do not know-or at any rate if it were allowed in every case it would just mean that those in business, including veterans of the last war, it must be remembered, would be deprived of part of the stocks in trade they would1 ibe able to obtain otherwise, because there is quite a scramble now for stocks in trade in these limited lines. So that some sort of reasonable balance has to be fixed. As I say, on the statement of facts given by the hon. gentleman there has been a delay for which there would appear to be no justification, and I shall have that case looked into at once.

What
would be the attitude of the board with respect to a case like this? A well established retailer dies and there is no one in the immediate family to carry on the business. The widow must sell. Would a permit be issued to a purchaser to take over that business? Of course these questions are always based on individual cases, and I understand there was such a case in which a permit was first refused and subsequently granted. I should like to know the practice.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am told that the practice is to grant permits in cases of transfers of ownership.
I think that would be fair.

I am sorry I was out of the house this morning, on account of the various committees which are sitting, and which I think is unfortunate, but I want to ask the minister something about the purchasing abroad of various commodities in bulk. Perhaps that question was answered earlier.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No. If my hon. friend will permit me, we are trying to finish up the item that was passed last night, and we shall come to the Commodity Prices Stabilization Corporation in a moment.
I thought the other item was finished last evening.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It was finished, but on the understanding that I would answer one or two questions that were raised, and I shall do that now.

Has the minister given consideration to the situation which I have brought up in the house on two different occasions, namely the application of the price ceiling along the border of New Brunswick and the absence of a price ceiling in the United States? I would urge the government to deal with that situation. Since I spoke previously in this connection a very difficult situation has arisen with respect to fuel wood along the border; I think I mentioned the matter months ago. Fuel wood is subject to a ceiling in New Brunswick. Fuel wood has no ceiling in the adjacent state of Maine. To-day the spectacle is being witnessed down there of truckload after truckload of fuel wood going across the line, commanding the higher price plus a premium. Last night at McAdam Junction a man who lives at Aroostook Junction told me that it was impossible to buy .fuel wood in New Brunswick as a result of that situation. A controller has been appointed down there. Has a permit system been set up, or what is the position? As the cold weather approaches that situation will become very serious, and of course the pulpwood situation is much more serious.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The hon. gentleman brought up the question of pulpwood, the export of which is under permit. Of course in connection with any commodity the price of which is higher in the United States than in Canada, very difficult questions arise because the exporters who are lucky enough to be able to get their exports under the quota permitted receive more money than those who are unlucky and have to sell in Canada.

That is not the difficulty. The quota is so large that it will take all our exports; there is no trouble about getting a permit. The difficulty is that the local mills are not going to be able to keep going. All the pulpwood cut on the farmers' lots and in the small freehold sections of the province is going into Maine, while the portion ordinarily available to the provincial mills is not available now because they cannot meet the price. There is no trouble about getting a permit to export.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
According to the figures I have, the situation is that Canada agreed to supply to the United States 1,550,000 cords of

War Appropriation-Prices Stabilization
pulpwood in the calendar year 1943, inasmuch as Canada for many years has been a substantial exporter of pulpwood to that country. Realizing the possibility of a reduction in production, this quantity was arrived at in relation to our exports of both pulpwood and newsprint, and compares with exports in 1942 of 1,920,508 cords and in 1941 of 1,842,234 cords. This reduction in quantity was arranged in order to allow a greater quantity of wood pulp to be available to Canadian consumers. With regard to wood fuel, that comes under the jurisdiction of the Minister of Trade and Commerce, and I am told that pulpwood comes under his jurisdiction as well.
I think that is correct.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am under the impression that fuel wood has not been placed under export permit.
That is right.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Perhaps it should be; I do not know.

From the investigations I have made I think that something in the nature of a permit system could be worked out under which the local controller who is on the ground could see that supplies for local consumers were reserved for them before the surplus was allowed to go out. However, the difficulty is the difference between the selling price in New Brunswick and the very much higher price across the line. The result is that producers just will not sell locally; they will take their chances on holding. I know it is a problem, perhaps due to the failure-I say that for lack of a better word- on the part of the authorities across the line to keep prices down somewhere on a parity with ours. The effect is very bad upon our consuming population, and this problem will have to be tackled.
I do not think the person who prepared that memorandum on pulpwood visualized the true position. It is true that we have always sent a certain amount of pulpwood, but when that was done we were dealing on an equal basis with the Maine mills. However, with the present ceiling price in Canada we just cannot compete with the prices they are willing to pay. No one is willing to sell to the Canadian mills. They know that we are well within the quota and they can ship across the line and get the enhanced price of at least $5 per cord; taking into account the premium, it may be even higher than that. This situation, if not
corrected, will result in at least one mill temporarily suspending operations. I am quite aware that we owe something to our United States friends in the way of supplies of raw materials, but this is the situation that exists.
I think the remedy would be to put a limitation on our price and let our people go out and compete with them on even terms. That may not be possible, but that is my suggestion. Let them take their chances on getting their share of the production. This is what should have been done at the beginning. Give them export permits, but let them compete on an equal basis.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Raise the price.

I am not suggesting that; perhaps there should be an increase in the price in New Brunswick, but that would be one more item of increased production costs. The minister talks about the cost of living, but the fact is that it is going up in every line. One item is the increased cost of producing pulpwood.. I am going to send the minister a copy of a letter which I received1 from a Methodist minister in Windsor about the increased cost of living and the price ceiling. It will amuse the minister to read this. I am not going to put it on the record. Say what you will, commend the policy, and I do commend its objectives, the fact remains that this thing is just bursting. I do not know how we are going to hold it without control across the line. It is a terrible problem that is confronting the board having regard to the situation existing in the United States. We are right alongside the border and we are feeling the repercussions.
It is not good enough to say that the cost of living index has not risen beyond what the minister says it has. Every housewife knows differently. If the minister were marketing, as I was on Saturday, and had to pay fifty cents a pound for lamb he would know what the cost of living is.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I will read the letter. I ask my hon. friend to read the remarks I made last night about the cost of living index.
I will. I know the minister defended it. He said that it was the best that was available, but that is a change in his attitude. He always said that it was the criterion.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do now.

I do not agree with the minister, and there is no one else in the world who does. It may be the
4510	COMMONS
War Appropriation-Prices Stabilization
best index that is available, but it does not tell the true story of the cost of living. Go into any home you like in this country and you will find that the cost of living has increased by a greater percentage than that given by the minister.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The cost of food has gone up thirty per cent.
The cost of everything else has gone up.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Not at all.
The cost of firewood has gone up twenty-five per cent.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: What proportion of your income do you spend on firewood?
In my case it might not be very much, but it would be quite large in the homes of some of the poor. The hon. member for St. Antoine-Westmount would not understand that.
What basis is used in allotting the percentage to food products?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Could we not finish the wartime prices and trade board item and then go on to the Commodity Prices Stabilization Corporation? I think when I answer two or three questions which I undertook to answer it should wind up the discussion on that item.
The hon. member for Kamloops (Mr. O'Neill) asked last night whether all the inspected slaughter houses were owned by the big packers. I have made inquiries and I find that there are 54 inspected slaughter houses in Canada, of which eighteen are owned by the big three packers, that is, Canada Packers, Swifts and Burns. The rest are owned by what might be called independents.
The hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker) asked the number of permits which had been granted to new entrants in business. In the first few months of the administration of the governing order it was not practicable to tabulate totals of permits issued. The figures could be obtained by a detailed analysis of the files, but this would represent a very large task. From March 16, 1943 on records have been kept which show that from that date to June 30, 689 permits have been issued. A large number of these have been for quite small enterprises; for example, 122 permits for egg grading stations and 31 for coal dealers. Permits issued prior to March 16 were for the most part granted in recognition of commitments made prior to November 2, in accordance with the policy announced when the order was issued. The

tion. member asked for the distribution of permits by provinces. There are four districts, and the distribution was as follows:
Western provinces	 360
Ontario	 178
Quebec	 106
Maritime	provinces	 45
The larger number in the western provinces is due to three factors. One, quite a number of egg grading stations were authorized; two, a large number of people were given the right to mix and sell mixed feed for live stock and poultry, and, three, it was necessary tO' authorize a number of new businesses to take care of the new Alaska project. The records of the director of licensing do not show separate figures for each western province.
The -hon. gentleman also asked for the figures showing the effect upon retail stores. Particulars as to the closures of retail establishments are not available, but the figures for commercial failures, as published by the Dominion Bureau of Statistics, diow the following for the trade and service groups:
1938		 776
1939		 861
1940		 792
1941		 671
1942		 522
The corresponding figure for 1931 was 1,357.
These figures, of course, do not tell the whole story, since there are a substantial number of persons retiring from trade otherwise than by failure. Figures for the total number of closures of retail establishments are not available, but the wartime prices and trade board has, on three occasions in the past year, arranged for test surveys to be made of the reasons for closures, examining approximately 150 cases on each occasion.
These surveys were made on recognized sampling techniques, and I have every reason to suppose that they reflect conditions generally. The surveys show conclusively that by far the greatest number of closures are still occasioned by reasons of illness, old age, and bad management, but quite a number are due to transfers into war industry and other civilian employment.
Some closures were reported as being due to curtailment of supplies. This is inevitable during war time, and must follow from the restrictions on manufacture of certain consumers' durable goods.
There has apparently been some increase in the closures occasioned for these reasons; the fact remains, however, that the greatest number of closures are still occasioned by reasons other than war-time controls.

The hon. member for Lake Centre asked for the number of directives that have been issued pursuant to the announced statement of policy on equitable distribution of goods in short supply.
This policy is implemented by all administrators of the wartime prices and trade board, and no centralized record of the directives given by such administrators is maintained, nor would it be practicable to do so. Any person who is of the opinion that he is not receiving his fair share of goods in accordance with the announced policy may apply to the appropriate administrator for relief, and if the administrator is satisfied, appropriate action is taken. Frequently such action is quite informal and an official directive is not necessarily issued.
The hon. member for Saskatoon City (Mr. Bence), suggested that there had been a deteijoration in quality of gasoline without a corresponding reduction in price. The standardization of grades of gasoline is covered by oil controller's order No. 008-A, dated September 26, 1941, which date is prior to the commencement of the over-all price ceiling.

Mr. O'NEILL: I do not want to hold up the minister's estimates, but a quota as between companies who had formerly done business is not, in my opinion, a fair way to have it. If you are going to operate it on a quota or percentage of what these men slaughtered last year or in 1941, you are going to squeeze out the small producer. There is no doubt about that.

I want to add a few remarks about the administration. There is a grave danger in the rapid expansion of this wartime prices administration, which went from $55,000 to $161,000, to $10,514,000, and now to $14,300,000 a year. By this rapid expansion in geometrical progression you are creating a mechanism which is not only inflationary in the widest sense but very possibly will not attain the objects for which it was created. It is fraught with great danger to the finances of the country in other ways and to all connected with the system. Just look over the many phases of the problem which has been discussed in the past twenty-four hours with regard to some twelve different forms of business. One cannot expect the Minister of Finance to know everything about this particular organization; it amazes me that he can attend to as much as he does. I do not want to be critical of him; I hope he has not inferred from what I said the other evening that I am critical of him and his department. But in a report made by a very important bank they point out that the more expensive and elaborate an administration becomes, the greater the opportunity for mistakes, and the more costly the mistakes, the greater is the inflationary effect. That is true. Anyone who has had any experience in this connection knows it to be true as subsidies tend to widen and cover more producers cost increase. There 
is a great deal of information on the administrative part of the board's work in a very informative bluebook covering the period September 1939 to March 1943.
From the various references which have been made in this debate one can see how widely this work has expanded. One hon. member has just referred to slaughtering, another has spoken of fluctuations in the cost of living affecting many very important phases of production and distribution. The system has widened out to something we never thought of. What I am fearful of is that we shall go a little too far. There was a return brought down on March 18 last, and I think the minister stated that, so far as the economic administration of this department and the economic life of our country were concerned, this had been turned over entirely to an outside board with such complete control that it was practically a parliament in itself. The head of it could issue rules and regulations having the force of statutes, with the grave dangers which attend such a proceeding. When the board started I asked certain questions of the minister concerning the expansion all along the line of this administration, which now costs $14,300,000. The higher you soar into the clouds of finance the less the likelihood that the money will be well spent. That is a well known economic principle.
On March 18 last I asked this question:

That is a very dangerous practice. True it is that there is a war on, but I am sorry to see what is going on in the name of the war. All over the country we find activities alleged to be for the war which are not for the war at all. I am surprised to see that the war is blamed for many expansions in the administration with which it has nothing to do.

The next question is, what are the salaries, living allowances, et cetera, of each official of the board, and what was his previous occupation? From the answer it is clear that a large number of lawyers and others were brought into the department as counsel, solicitors, administrators, assistants in the price division, and deputy administrators. They must have a very large legal busines to judge by the amount of money spent on legal costs. As to the administration of rentals, more than sixty per cent of it is just a farce. The minute the man who got the position is appointed what does he do? He heads for Chicago to address a real estate convention. Then they have a "special assistant to newsprint administrator." Of course they have press officers who, I know, beset the newspaper offices. I know that myself, from the unfair and untrue criticism I have had in the past two or three years from certain of the corporation press in one part of Canada. The secretary of the board is answerable to the chairman, we are told in the return. I do not know anybody who was not answerable to the chairman. I do not think the chairman is answerable to anyone in the heavens above or the earth beneath or the waters under the earth. Is there anything in that important agency, from beginning to end, which the chairman of the board is not over? Then there is the chief of supply. He is loaned from the foreign exchange control board. There are many other administrative officers, but I will not detain the committee by reading a list of them. I find that hardly any of these men know anything at all about what they are trying to administer, or have any practical 72537-2861
experience in it whatever and never had. As I said the other day in connection with the administration of beef and butter, all they know about beef and butter is what they consume themselves. We find doctors of everything, lawyers, clerks, preachers and everybody else brought into the department to handle the business, economic and all else, of this organization. Would anybody here engage a Doctor of Laws to manage -his wholesale business? No. Doctors of Law are all right in their sphere, but certainly this is not their sphere. Go over the whole department and you will find similar occasions for criticism. The chairman, the administrator of this department, with a payroll of $14,000,000 is himself a civil servant. I have never yet said in this chamber anything of a personal nature about a man, and I do not intend to begin now.
They are all gentlemen, as far as I know. There is one very fine man sitting at the table now, and I would probably not have said as much as I did had I been aware of the fact. But the public principle is just the same no matter where these gentlemen sit, whether here in the gallery or behind desks in an office. They are passing orders that affect the liberties of the subject and a lot of what is done is doing little or nothing to win the war. I can say that this sort of thing has been condemned in the British House of Commons and an attempt is being made there to get away as much as possible from it. The other day I referred to what is being done at the present time in Washington. They do not want to have any such elaborate system of controls there. We had an example of it in the new deal idea which was introduced by Professor Moley of Cleveland into the United States some years ago, and this method of erecting artificial barriers and all kinds of barriers in the way of business was condemned in that country before the war. They saw something of what was coming in this war and they are trying now to reduce administrative machinery in the senate there as far as they possibly can instead of expanding it as we are doing here. The more it expands and widens in Canada, the greater the likelihood of the whole system collapsing, because we are simply building on sand and when the rains descend, and the winds come, and the floods rise, woe betide the taxpayer of Canada, the retailer, the wholesaler and all the little business men throughout the country.
The small stores are being closed up right and left. In my own constituency 18 per cent of these small establishments have gone out of business, and I have been told by responsible
4514	COMMONS
War Appropriation-Prices Stabilization
persons that this figure will rise to anywhere from 20 to 40 per cent. Going down on the street car on Yonge street I can see buildings in which small stores used to flourish and which are now converted to other housing uses. There was one fish store in Toronto that had been carrying on business for thirty years and now it has been turned by conversion into a three-family apartment. I do not know how people can possibly live in a place from which the smell of fish cannot possibly have been removed after all that time. All these little stores are being put out of business by this board.
The chairman himself was a civil servant, and what does he do? He gets first a skeleton staff, two or three civil servants of the second class, around him and then appoints outsiders. I do not wish to say anything to disparage the civil service. Far from it. I think we have an excellent civil service in this country. From that service some men have gone into business outside and have risen to the top. One such man has made a success of the banking business and is head of a bank to-day. He used to be in the Department of Finance. Our civil service has been a blessing to the taxpayers of Canada. These able men have worked for comparatively small salaries all their lives and have effected a great deal of economy in the country's administration. We have one able man at the table to-day, and there are many in the minister's department. But after selecting a skeleton staff they go to the universities to get their men. One favourite university is that in Hamilton, McMaster, a fine university. I remember when it used to be on Bloor street in Toronto, and I can say that it has turned out some very able men, for example, Mr. Cyrus Eaton of Cleveland, a Canadian, a man of outstanding ability and a credit to this country. But this board gets together a lot of professors, doctors, lawyers and other professional men and marches them into the office before the chairman and he assigns them to duties all over the country.
They have virtually assumed kingly powers over the citizens of Canada and over parliament, and they issue their edicts every day. Municipal officials are constantly writing to me from various parts of Ontario asking me what this or that order in council means, but no Philadelphia lawyer could tell them what the law is. They have drawn for a staff on the genius of a cosmopolitan collection of self-styled patriots, because that is all they are, who have left their chairs in college and their teaching, their offices and their desks in Toronto, Hamilton, and also here, to serve the state, if you please, at
(Mr. Church.]
two or three times the salary that an able civil servant receives. They are disrupting the whole civil service by such favouritism. And added to that, they receive travelling expenses,, hotel bills, and so on. When I travel on the trains I can see the sort of accommodation provided for them compared with what ordinary civilians have to put up with.
It would not be so bad if these gentlemen knew anything at all about 'business, retail or wholesale, or about technical questions which they seek as amateurs to control and which they presume to dispose of. As I read a list of these gentlemen, from beginning to end, I am reluctantly driven to the conclusion that generally speaking they are chosen by the chairman of the board on the principle that they have no knowledge whatever of the work they are asked to undertake. And what do they do? They begin by driving out of business all the small storekeepers and retailers on Bloor street, Yonge street and elsewhere, all the little producers and dealers, and muddle all production and distribution. They are driving all these people to distraction with the number of orders they issue directing experienced men how to run their business. Last night I referred to clothing. Well, these gentlemen are telling people engaged in the retail and wholesale business exactly how to run their affairs, and the result is that to-day we have a sort of tower of Babel.
They issue their orders every day over the radio and in full-page advertisements in the newspapers, and some of the corporation press will not publish one word of criticism of them. Instead of that they write pages of articles eulogizing these many control gentlemen and their sisters and cousins and aunts. And the writers of such articles do not publish their initial names as formerly. A lot of these people have adopted the hyphened compound name. Suppose some gentleman who used to be known as John K. Doorhandle is appointed an administrator; thereafter he becomes John Knob-Doorhandle. In some instances where the state takes over a business from private enterprise, these men step in to control and to direct businesses that have been managed by the same family people for two or three generations. These bureaucrats step in and dictate to the son or the grandson of some man who established a well known business two generations ago, and, let us say, which has been running successfully all these years. The bureaucrats come in and destroy it by their amateur mistakes. The result is that private enterprise is nowhere to-day, because the private business man is not allowed any

War Appropriation-Prices Stabilization
longer to use his own initiative. He must obey the dictates of this new form of civil service bureaucracy that has sprung up in the country and knows not how to operate a competent business.
I submit that we are allowing this modern bureaucracy too much leeway. The deputy subcontroller has to report to the subcontroller, and the subcontroller to the controller and the controller to somebody else, so that there is no finality about anything. Weeks and months pass before you can get anything done or any finality along any line. The man in private business gets results and he will admit his mistakes when he makes any, but not these gentlemen. I do not believe in this expansion system; we have had too much of it and, as I said last night, I believe there should be some curtailment of it, although a lot of good work has been done so far. This item of administration has now .reached 814,300,000. I do not know what auditing of this amount there can be. For two years I have been trying to find out who has control of the department, whether it is the comptroller of the treasury or the auditor general. These are war appropriation items, and all the comptroller of the treasury has to do is to put his stamp on them, without any investigation at all. The auditor general wrote me a letter last year in which he said, "I have no control over these war appropriation bills." He deals only with civil estimates.
I can tell you we are heading for disaster. I have not made any strenuous objection, because I believe the minister is overburdened with work. I believe, too, that he has done a great deal of good work in the prevention of the inflationary spiral. I am prepared to admit that. May I add that he has the backing of the large majority of the people of this country in what he has done so far to control inflation; but surely the time has come when we should change our policy of dealing with the whole problem. Let us do something to help wholesale and retail business men. I say this because there are many small retail business men in my constituency, and I have been deeply impressed by what I have heard people say.
For instance, I have in mind one business on Eastern avenue which has operated for almost a 'hundred years. But they have now been driven to the wall, and1 have had to close up. There are many poor people in my constituency, because it is very largely a workingman's community. I deeply sympathize with them, when they come to me and tell me that families which never knew what it was to be haled into police courts, families whose records have been clean
for three generations, have now been subjected to that sort of treatment, for some petty infraction.
I did not say what the newspapers reported with respect to prosecutions. I said in the return I read there were 150 in the two years and nine months, 96 of which were from Ontario mostly Toronto. The minister gave the figures correctly when he placed them on Hansard. There were 3,355 prosecutions from December 1, 1941, to May 31, 1943. There were 894 for infractions of the price control regulations, 952 for infractions of the rental regulations, 465 against the rationing regulations, and 225 prosecutions of other kinds. Then, there were 467 prosecutions in connection with the sale of gasoline, 263 in connection with tires, and 65 other prosecutions. Then, if we deduct the figures 150 which I gave for the first two years and nine months we have a figure of 3,205 prosecutions in the last fiscal year.
I do not wish to detain the committee further. I 'have always been opposed to this censorship business. I do not blame the minister for it, or the chairman of the board. But I do know that some of these press officers are going into the newspaper offices to attack those here who dare criticize-at least, I have been told that by newspaper men. I have great respect for the minister and his department, and his fine parliamentary assistant. I exempt them. But I do sympathize with those people who have been driven out of business by drastic controls. Businesses have been operating for two or three generations and they have gone to the wall. Some of their sons are at war. Of course those people hope to hold their business. I attended a funeral the other day of a man whose business had been in the family for three generations. Three of that man's sons are overseas. The father is dead, and when they come back they will not have a business. They will have no business to conduct when they return. I do plead with the minister to put on the brakes on some of these controls that will not aid the war and will lead to inflation. I would ask him to have the board put on the brakes, so that we may have some private initiative, thrift and enterprise, and an opportunity of conducting wholesale and retail business, and small business, not only in Toronto, but in other cities throughout Canada.

As I understand it the government to-day is controlling the importation of these commodities. Is that done through a government organization, or is it done, as I believe it is, through brokers? speechtext: The best answer to a question like that would be a reference to the report of the wartime prices and trade board.
I am sorry I have not read it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
It is a good foundation for any discussion with respect to these matters. At page 29 I find the following:
The third method by which the government has taken a share of a "squeeze" too heavy to be absorbed by industry and trade has been through purchases by the Commodity Prices Stabilization Corporation of Canadian requirements of certain imports from abroad. In general the corporation sells such imports at prices appropriate to the retail ceiling. It is selling tea, for example, at a price appropriate to the reduced retail price announced in accordance with the cost of living reduction programme. Coffee has been sold at a price appropriate to the ceiling in spite of cost' increases, although now these cost increases, as well as the 4 cents a pound reduction on retail sales to consumers, have been offset by cancellation of the special war duty. Despite increased costs the selling prices of other bulk purchases, among them cocoa beans, bristles, beeswax, spices, dried fruits, fertilizers, pesticides, oils and fats, and certain types of cotton fabrics, have also been set in appropriate relation to retail ceiling prices. Economies resulting from centralized buying through a single government agency have made it possible to keep trading losses to a minimum. Trading losses incurred by the Commodity Prices Stabilization Corporation up to February 28, 1943, totalled $2,111,383.28.

That is not the point in which I am particularly interested. I was wondering just how this business is conducted. Do we buy and sell through brokers, or does the commodity control board have its own organization, or does it designate certain brokers, or just what is done in this regard?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
A question was asked about this company by the hon. member for St. Jolm+Albert on February 4, 1943, to which an answer was given on March 3, as follows:
1.	Do Harrisons and Crosfield (Canada) Limited act as brokers for Commodity Prices Stabilization Corporation?
A. No.
2.	Is this company employed by the corporation in any other capacity?
A. Yes; as the managing agents of the bulk purchasing division of the corporation, their responsibilities being to arrange for procurement of the goods and thereafter take all necessary action to ensure delivery.

3.	How long has it been employed as broker or in any other capacity with the corporation, and on whose recommendation was it appointed?
A. In the above capacity, since March 1, 1942; directly by the corporation at its own instance.
4.	Is this company the exclusive broker for the corporation, and if not how many other persons or companies are so employed, and what are their names and addresses?
A. No; bulk purchases by the corporation are distributed as far as possible through ordinary trade channels which may include the use of brokers.
5.	What remuneration does this company receive for its services to the corporation, and what service has it rendered the corporation to date, and how much has it been paid in each case?
A. The contract with the corporation provides that Harrisons and Crosfield (Canada) Limited assumes the cost of office, travelling, salaries and other charges (except office space and stenographic assistance at the head office of the corporation), such expenses to be reimbursed to Harrisons and Crosfield out of commissions covered by the following schedule. These commissions are calculated on the f.o.b. port of shipment price, i.e., on the prime cost, exclusive of transportation, duty, insurance and similar charges:
Up to	$ 100,000-2i per cent
Over $ 100.000 but under	250,000-2 per cent
Over 250,000 but under	500,000-1J per cent
Over 500,000 but under 1,000,000-1 per cent Over 1,000,000	- i per cent
Harrisons and Crosfield (Canada) Limited are required to keep separate accounts for expenses incurred exclusively in connection with the corporation's business. To the extent that the net earnings of Harrisons and Crosfield (Canada) Limited, including profits from the contract with the corporation, bring the total profits of the company above the profits subject to income taxes earned in the company's fiscal year ended April 30, 1942, such earnings on the corporation's business will be rebated. Under this general arrangement definite settlement has been made up to September 30, 1942. For the four months which have elapsed since that date advances amounting to a total of $20,000 have been made, subject to final accounting and adjustment which, under the agreement described above, takes place quarterly but is naturally delayed on account of the necessity to prepare statement of profit and loss for each quarter. The agreement came into effect about 1st March, 1942, and the total cost for the seven months ending September 30 was $47,017.42 which, as indicated, includes all salaries, travelling, office and other expenses. This covers a total turnover during the period of approximately $15,000,000. The total cost of the period was therefore less than one-third of one per cent of the turnover, the limiting factor mentioned above having had the effect of reducing the commissions which would otherwise have been payable under the above schedule for this seven months by no less than $96,080.42.
The services rendered the corporation is covered by the answer to question No. 2. It will be seen from the above explanation that the cost of services cannot be apportioned to individual transactions.

6.	What is the total amount this company has been paid to date for services rendered the corporation?
A. Up to September 30, 1942, Harrisons and Crosfield (Canada) Limited have received payments as mentioned above of $47,017.42. For the four months ending January 31, 1943, the company have received advances of $20,000, subject to accounting and adjustment on a quarterly basis, as explained above.
7.	Is this company employed in any other capacity by the government or any board or other corporation set up by the government and if so, by what department, board or other corporation and in what capacity and how much has it received to date for its services?
A. No information.

The import subsidies are

There seems to be a good
deal of fear that the price level in the United States may cause a rise in our price ceiling, but so long as we continue our subsidies it should not materially affect Canada because on balance the exports would gain- by the amount that we lose on our imports. We would not suffer at all provided we carried on our subsidies to maintain the price ceiling.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
That is quite theoretical,
and I do not know whether I can give an answer. If prices went up very high in the United States, our subsidy bill would be very great. The payment of subsidies is an inflationary influence in itself, nevertheless we feel that it is desirable because it is not nearly as productive of inflation as letting prices go uncontrolled would be.
How can the minister say that it is inflationary in view of the fact that it is used for the purpose of reducing prices?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is the spending of government money, it increases the purchasing power and it puts an additional strain upon the ceiling of prices. It is used to hold them there; nevertheless it puts an upward strain on them.
But on the other hand you are obtaining a large part of that by taxation, which would have a deflationary effect; it should counterbalance the other.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: If we could get everything back by taxation there would be no difficulty; there would be nothing inflationary about the payments being made, but of course we cannot do that. We can get some of it back; we can get a lot of it by borrowing, but it does not work perfectly by any means.

In view of the fact that we are having trouble in maintaining a price ceiling, would it not foe a good thing to eliminate the sales tax, which would give relief to the extent of 8 per cent, and then substitute direct taxation for the sales tax?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I would not be in favour of that, because we have so much difficulty with direct taxation. Hon. members are familiar with the problems that income taxation creates. We are told by creditable sources all over Canada that because of the progressive factor of the income tax, higher earnings being charged a greater rate, the working of overtime is discouraged and there is greater absenteeism, with a resultant diminishing production. If we raised our income taxes sufficiently to make up for what we would lose by repealing the sales tax, the undesirable features of the income tax would be accentuated. After all, the sales tax takes purchasing power back from people who I think can now afford to pay.
But it falls most heavily upon people who are in the low income brackets, because it takes a greater proportion of their income.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It seems to be regarded as perfectly natural and normal that a man in the lower income brackets will not wish to work if most or a large part of his pay is taken in taxes. But it seems to be considered an abnormal and shocking thing if a man in the high income brackets should act in the same way.

It is the amount that is left after the taxation is applied that really counts, and the amount that is left to people in the higher income brackets, even after the heavy taxation is applied to their incomes, is much higher than what is left to the people in the lower income brackets.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Whether we like it or not, you cannot possibly level the standard of living of everybody in the country. The organization of society is such that it is impossible.
You can at least make it more equitable in time of war.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is exactly what we have done, and done to a tremendous degree.
I understood the minister to say that the amount paid to this particular firm in commission averaged one-third of one per cent.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: On the turn-over.

Yes. In view of those figures I cannot see how the average could be one-third of one per cent.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: There is profit control.
That is where profit control enters?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Now, Mr. Chairman, let me correct two or three statements of my hon. friend.
In the first place, the ceiling of thirty-five and thirty-six cents is not the retail ceiling; it is the ceiling on the price which the creamery can charge the jobber or wholesaler or anyone else who buys from the creamery in solid blocks of fifty-six pounds and in carload lots. When we talk about a thirty-five or thirty-six cent ceiling, that is the ceiling. To that must be added the wholesale mark-up, the charges for cutting and wrapping, the retail markup, and transportation.
Is there any control on these points?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The control there is the retail ceiling, and the retail ceiling is the highest price for which that individual retailer sold butter in the period between September 15 and October 11, 1941. There are individual retail ceilings. That is the principle of the price ceiling policy; it varies from place to place; it may vary between stores in the same city; it may be forty-three cents in one store and forty-two cents in another.
And fifty-three cents in another.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The man who charged the fifty-three cents would not stay in business; he would not sell any butter.
Unless the other fellows were out.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is right, if by some miracle some butter seller in Sydney were able to get fifty-three cents in the base period, but I do not believe there is one in Sydney or anywhere else in Canada.
I am not saying that there is, but it is not so long since there was.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: If there were, the law would permit him to go up to that retail ceiling, because that is the ceiling. I think I have made that clear about the butter.

These ceiling prices
apply only to persons who buy in blocks of fifty-six pounds and in carload lots?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.
So that a small dealer in butter could not take advantage of this, could he? I mean he could not buy less than a carload and he would have to have the equipment to deal with it by the block.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: What happens there is that there are recognized differentials. He would probably pay half a cent more.
Could the minister give a break-down of this $120,000,000?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: YTs. I should, however, like to talk a little longer to my fellow Nova Scotian, the hon. member for Cape Breton South.
You were giving the Minister of Agriculture information that time, not me.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not think so. I think the Minister of Agriculture understands it pretty well.

He was stuck at the thirty-six cents.
