speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Yes, but he was stuck at the creamery too; he was not at the grocery store in Sydney.
My hon.. friend made some rather sweeping statements about these munitions and supply people buying from themselves. That is his theory, but it really is not the situation. He talked about controllers. The controllers do not do any buying at all. That is not what a controller does. He does not buy. The persons who do the buying are those in the purchasing division. My hon. friend may think and may say that officers of the purchasing divisions are buying from themselves. I do not know who constitute the purchasing divisions, but I myself believe that the buyers of the Department of Munitions and Supply are extremely conscientious buyers. That is my conviction.
That is what I am afraid of.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: If my hon. friend is afraid of it, let me tell him what he had better do. He can get all the orders in council and he can there get the purchases and the prices. We have to put through a great many orders in council, a thousand or so a month.. Not all have to do with buying; but purchases of over $15,000 have to be passed by the governor in council, and if anybody wants to challenge the prices being paid by the Department of Munitions and Supply, why does he not challenge them head-on and say, "That is too high; that is more than the stock is worth." But do not come at it in this way and accuse these men of breach of trust, because that is what it is, when my hon. friend says that men have got themselves appointed- here to a public position, and act in this way in the discharge of their duties. They are servants of the government. My hon. friend said they were not, but they are servants of the crown and they have positions of trust. He should not accuse these men of violating their trust unless he has some facts to go on. He should not go on just what he thinks they would do or what he thinks somebody might do, because I do not believe they are doing it.
The minister has already made statements to this committee which prove that they are doing it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: What?

Forcing the price ceiling. They are granted privileges which the ordinary citizen of this country is not granted. And second, if I come in here from Canada Packers or International Nickel or Barclays Bank and am on loan to the government of this country for a year or tw-o years, I am 
going back to my former position. That is where my future means of livelihood is. And we are all human.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: We are not human in that sense.
I am expressing my opinion. It is still my opinion, and I think it is the opinion of a large percentage of the people of the country.
Oh, no.

Oh, yes. If a corporation outside this house is paying me $25,000 a year and I come here and take a position on this board, my first consideration, is to protect that company I am working for. That is human. Neither the Minister of Finance nor the Minister of Munitions and Supply has any more control -over such a man than I have, because he can walk off the job to-morrow and he is not losing anything. He is not obligated to the government or to the people of the country. As I see the whole set-up, I am not quarrelling with the minister or making accusations, but I am giving my opinion on the basis of what I know of human nature and of the responsibilities of those on the inside to those on the outside. I say that the latitude given munitions and supply is too sweeping. It is too much control in the hands of somebody who has something to sell, who is not responsible to the taxpayers of Canada by virtue of election and the necessity of reporting upon his stewardship. They report to the boards of directors of corporations. T am not making accusations.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes, you are.

I am pointing out the;
implications of the machinery.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The hon. gentleman has a very low view of human nature. I am really surprised. To begin with, people do not act in that way. Just the odd one does. The average person does not. When he accepts a position with the government of Canada he does not act in that way. I do not know whether they all have to take an oath, but they do in the wartime prices and trade board. Does the hon. member not give them credit for wanting to do something from good motives?
If they take a position with the government, but not otherwise.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
But they take a position with the government and are answerable to their deputy minister and their minister and the presumption is that they will do their -duty. If my hon. friend wanted to ascribe

War Appropriation-Prices Stabilization
a low motive to these men, I would point out that what they do is open to the scrutiny of official after official in a long line, and finally it comes to the government. If a man were of that type and dared to try that sort of thing there, he would be spotted in a day or a week and it would be well known that he was not the kind of man to have in the employ of the government. I say to my hon. friend that instead of propounding his remarkably low views of human nature, and therefrom deducing that men are acting in certain ways, he should tell me what they have done that is wrong. Let him tell the Minister of Munitions and Supply what they did that is wrong and we will face it here. But do not base it on some idea of an essential badness and a disposition toward a breach of duty, a breach of trust, which I am satisfied does not exist in the case of the great majority of persons employed by the government. Most of these people are proud of the job they are doing. The important thing for them is not some crooked back-door favour that they can do their former employers. The important thing for some of them is the prestige they gain by doing a great war-time job. Surely my hon. friend has enough imagination; surely there is enough scope in his understanding of the motives that prompt people, to realize that. Surely he does not think that men come here and take jobs, making great sacrifices in many instances, in order to put their own sordid, mercenary financial motives above these other and higher considerations. As a matter of fact they do not. I am satisfied that they do not, and the rank and file of the people of the country, I think, will agree with me rather than with my hon. friend. The trouble with my hon. friend, and with some others in this house, is that they think, if men are earning more than a small income, there is something crooked about them. They think that is the case. That is not my experience. I have said repeatedly in this house that in the low-income groups, as in the high-income groups, there are good men and bad men, and I have not been able to draw any hard and fast rule such as my hon. friend implies. The idea that because a man has made a success of his life and has accumulated some money, or has obtained a position wherein he makes a substantial income, he is a crook, is entirely false. My hon. friend says: oh, yes; but they pierced the ceiling in some cases. I cannot get the facts very well on this, but there was a time when, in order to get cattle, a year or two ago, they had to pay a good deal to obtain them for the reason that cattle were not coming forward.
They had to pay a lot to get cattle, but it does not follow that the people who provided the cattle got the prices.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Cattle were $12 on the
Toronto market, which was inappropriate to the ceiling, and there were sales to the department that were appropriate to that high price to the farmer.

Let us place this matter
in its proper perspective in relation to other questions. If that price was set and the farmers would not sell at that price, the farmers were on strike. What was said in this house when we were discussing the steel strike? One hon. member rose in his place and said, "I would have uniforms for these men and tell them to get into those uniforms or go to work." There was a great pounding of desks on that side of the house when that statement was made. It is all right, however, for Canada Packers to go on strike, or for Canada Packers to hold up the people of Canada until they got their prices. The department of munitions comes through and pays the price and nothing is said about it. When we were discussing the aluminum deal one after another said, "What could we do? These people have a monopoly of aluminum and if we did not pay their price we could not get aluminum." But when a worker takes the position that he is not getting enough to eat-not that he is not getting enough profit, which is an altogether different thing-after months and sometimes years of negotiations, after jumping over every hurdle which the government by order in council could think of, so that he is compelled as a last resort to go on strike, ministers do not stand up and make excuses for that man. We have to be fair about this. The minister may not believe that people are actuated by these sordid motives, but the leader of the opposition (Mr. Graydon)-and I do not find any opposition to him on that side of the house on this score-suggests that private initiative is the only way by which we can get things done; that there must be an incentive for people to make gains, or people will not work. My hon. friend was on the price spreads and mass buying commission that sat here in 1934 and 1935. Has he forgotten the report of that commission? Has he forgotten what they reported to the house? Yet he rises and says that we can leave this matter to business men and be assured that everything will be fair and aboveboard.
As a matter of fact no explanation has been given by the minister as to why the department of munitions should be allowed to

pay more than the ceiling price for any commodity. speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The instances of paying more than the price ceiling have not been very numerous. There has been a return to the house from the wartime prices and trade board. They have a working arrangement which in effect provides that the price ceiling shall not be exceeded by munitions and supply at least until after there is consultation with the wartime prices and trade board and they have attempted to get supplies for the Department of Munitions and Supply at or below the ceiling. The Department of Munitions and Supply have done, I think I am safe in saying, far more purchasing below the ceiling than they have above the ceiling. But they do have a certain freedom1 which is not permitted in connection with civilian purchases.
There is no law against anyone purchasing below the ceiling.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No, but they have a certain freedom. They can pay more; if it is necessary to pay a price higher than the ceiling price to get supplies, they have freedom to do it. I never said you could safely leave everything to business men and trust them always to do the right thing. I never said that at all.
That was the assumption.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No; that was not the assumption at all.

That is the general
assumption.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
No; that is not the general assumption, nor was it my assertion. With the system of checks and balances, and the number of officials through whom they have to go, finally reaching the governor in council in respect of purchases of more than $16,000, there is ample protection. The prices that are paid are not the prices known to one man alone, or to one man's company, or to a limited number of people. They are known to a whole lot of people. And the prices, I am satisfied, are not wrong. I should like to hear some talk on prices, instead of talk about people.
I Mr. MacInnis.J

I do not wish the minister to put words in my mouth. He tried to create the impression that I was making individual accusations, and that it was my endeavour to prove that these men were crooks. That word was used by no one but himself. I merely said that I objected to any organization or any group of people in this country having any special privileges under the laws of the country. That is what I objected to. I still contend that if I am drawing $25,000 a year from a company, and I am sent here to Ottawa, and not being paid anything for my work here, my main interest is that company which is employing me. It is their interests I am concerned with.
I also know-and I think the minister knows it too-that the war we are engaged in to-day has a lot to do with the control now set up in Canada, and the future of that control. I know that in Canada and in the United States and in Great Britain there is just as great a struggle going on on the home front to change the order of society to something that will suit those who are responsible for what is going on in Europe to-day. And Canada is not isolated from that struggle. She is not isolated from those who stand for that so-called system of private enterprise and the right to exploit our fellow-men. And those who stand for private enterprise are very carefully watching to see where there is any control that will influence the future of this country in that direction.
I sat in on meetings of the reconstruction committee, and in the last few months I have heard presentations from almost every organization in the country, including chambers of commerce, the legislative mouthpieces of big business who are in on these controls to-day.
I know what they represent and what their opinions are with respect to the future of Canada. I know what their opinions are with respect to democracy. I know the use to Which these controls will be put. I know what their intentions are with respect to crown companies, and the investments of the people to-day in plants and factories.
It is all these things, and the knowledge of what Canada faces in the future, that make me fearful of any control in this country on the part of any group of individuals other than the elected representatives of the people of Canada. I am afraid that in the not far distant future perhaps the Minister of Finance and other ministers may not have the right to sit in and to legislate for the people of Canada. That is what I am afraid of, and that is why I wish to see this parliament supreme in any matter involving the laws

War Appropriation-Prices Stabilization
of this country. I am interested in seeing that no freedom to go beyond those laws, in any way, is extended to any group of individuals.

The minister has said that he would like to hear an attack made upon prices. Perhaps I shall make an attack, but it may be different from what he might expect. I shall not attack the piercing of any price ceiling, but I would say something about prices which, in some parts of the country are regarded as being a little bit too low. I refer to farm prices.
I shall not make a speech, but will simply ask the minister if it is possible for him to inform us why the Canadian farmer must accept less for his wheat and less for many other products he produces than is received by the farmer in the United States? I have not heard an explanation on the point, despite the fact that I asked for one on an earlier occasion, and the subject has been discussed with the Minister of Agriculture. Perhaps the answer may be complicated; I do not know. But I do know that that is a question which has not been satisfactorily answered, so far as the farmers are concerned.
I have read that when speaking in Chicago not long ago the Minister of Agriculture said that the greatest problem which faced the government of Canada was that of explaining to Canadian farmers why they must take a dollar a bushel, or whatever the price of wheat might be, while the United States farmer was privileged to receive a considerably higher price. Then I believe he went on to say the answer was that we were all taking part in a great, united effort to win the war, and that there must be equality of sacrifice.
That is not a satisfactory answer, so far as equality of sacrifice is concerned. Not only does the farmer of western Canada take a lower price for his product than is received by the farmer in the United States, but he must pay more for his farm machinery' and those other necessary commodities he must buy to equip and run his farm. He has to pay much more than the farmer in the United States. This is the picture; the farmer in the United States pays less for his equipment and receives a bigger price for his product, "while the farmer in Canada receives less for his product and has higher operating costs. Yet we are all fighting the same war, and the desire is to have equality of sacrifice.
I do not know whether the minister can give a satisfactory answer, but those are the questions being asked. And, believe me, when Canadian farmers make up their income tax returns they will certainly ask those questions. I am sure they are questions vital to the
minister as well as to farmers, and I should like to know if he would give the committee an answer.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The hon. member has certainly opened up a big question. The question as to the level of farm prices has been discussed time and again, and I had hoped that at this time we might avoid another discussion, because once it is opened it might continue for a long time.
Farm prices in Canada are not as high as prices in the United States. Wages, generally speaking, are not as high in Canada as they are in the United States. Living costs are not nearly as high in Canada as in the United States, either. The United States is in a higher level all along the line than we are in Canada. The hon. member has said that some of the operating costs faced by farmers are lower in the United States than they are in Canada. I do not know whether that is correct or not.
What about farm machinery?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Probably farm machinery; I do not know about that. But I do not think that is true generally with respect to farm costs in the United States. I am certain also that farm costs have gone up faster and farther in the United States, by far, than they have in Canada since the beginning of the war. We have a different economy here. We cannot tie our economy to that of the United States. If we were to raise farm prices to United States levels, there would immediately have to be widespread wage increases all along the line-I do not mean the international line but all over the country-and if there were wage increases together with increases in the price of farm products, certainly those wage increases would lead to increases in the prices of all industrial products.
If the minister would permit a question, would it be necessary to raise wage rates if the increases in farm prices were paid by bonus or subsidy?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
There is a limit to subsidies. I could not reconcile myself to an unlimited laying out of subsidies. The subsidy policy is one which must be operated within limits; otherwise it would break down by the force of public opinion. Even in the United States apparently the senate will not pass a subsidy policy. To keep public opinion behind it a subsidy policy has to be kept within reasonable limits. If it starts soaring to great heights you are pouring out these vast amounts of money all over the country; the taxpayers are paying that money; it is going to farmers

War Appropriation-Prices Stabilization
and others. Theoretically it comes back in the form of income tax from the farmers, but actually it would not.

But the minister
would agree that, provided increases were met through subsidies, it would not necessarily result in an increase in wages?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not want to answer a question in theory or to make a theoretical answer.
But the minister is answering in theory. He is talking in theory right now; it is his theory.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am sorry if I am; I was trying to answer the question of the hon. member for Macleod.

I should like to know how the minister justifies the removal of the ten per cent war exchange tax on vegetables coming into' Canada, while not- removing that tax from the machinery necessary for the production of those vegetables in this country.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Our business is to keep prices stable, and with the exception of a minor adjustment at the beginning of the priceceiling policy the prices of farm machinery have not risen above the ceiling prices. We have taken great pains to see that this should be so. The price ceiling came in on December 1, 1941; thereafter the highest prices that could be charged were the highest prices of farm machinery during the period from September 15 to October 11, 1941. Certain prices had been raised before that, but one or two of the companies-I cannot remember which companies they were-had announced increases in prices but had not put those increases into effect before October 11, 1941, so that an increase of up to five per cent was permitted those companies in order to bring them into line with the other companies. From that time to this, however, prices of farm machinery have been stabilized, despite what would have been great increases in cost if stabilization measures had not been taken all the way down the line. The prices of farm machinery have been kept at that level.
With regard to fruits and vegetables, I would not say the price level has got out of hand in the United States, but at least it has gone away up in that country, so that, as hon. members know, cabbages, asparagus and all these other imported fruits and vegetables have sold in Canada at very high prices. We thought the time had come when we should do almost anything to bring down the prices of these fruits and vegetables. There was a reason for taking action there which did not apply in the other case.

Certainly prices of farm machinery have gone up since the start of the war. The higher exchange in the United States, together with the ten per cent war exchange tax has meant a straight twenty per cent increase in prices of farm machinery since this war started, and I think the government should take into consideration the question of removing that ten per cent tax.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: We are not talking about increases since the outbreak of the war; we are talking about the freezing period. If I were to talk about increases since the outbreak of war I could give some amazing figures about the percentage increases in the prices of farm products, but the moment I did that I would be accused of taking increases over a period of low-price levels. Farm prices have increased by forty-three 'per cent since 1939, or, excluding wheat, by fifty per cent, not counting butter fat subsidies. I could give a whole list of articles I have here, but prices of farm machinery have not gone up anything like those percentages since the beginning of the war. However, I do not think we would gain anything by going back to the beginning of the war. We go back to the freezing period between September 15 and October 11, 1941, and we have kept farm machinery prices to that level. We have gone to a great deal of trouble and expense to do that, and therefore there is not the same reason applying in that case as in the case of these fruits and vegetables that have gone sky-high as a result of not being under the ceiling in Canada. So far as I can see, they cannot be brought under the ceiling here, but in any event those higher prices have resulted from higher costs or lack of control or something in the United States.

How about the cost of farm machinery repairs?
Mr. ILSLEYr: They are under the ceiling.

Does the minister's statement with regard to the cost of farm machinery apply also to repairs to that machinery?
Mr. ILSLEYr: Y'es; under the ceiling they have not been raised at all; there has been no adjustment upwards. What I said about the one or two companies in regard to farm machinery does not apply to repairs, which are subject to the ceiling.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I do not wish to interfere with the hon. member for Wetaskiwin; if he is going to follow up this discussion I shall yield at once, but I wanted to ask one or two questions on a point already raised.

War Appropriation-Prices Stabilization

I have only one further question to ask. Does the minister consider that gold mining has any effect upon prices in Canada? By that I mean that the money distributed through the mining of gold is effective purchasing power, but nothing which the people consume is produced. I take it that the gold is exchanged to the United States for munitions; and since the value of our gold production is in the neighbourhood of $200,000,000 a year, I suppose that represents roughly the purchasing power that is distributed in Canada, in respect of which no consumable goods are produced. Therefore it increases the purchasing power without also increasing the supply of retail goods. I should like to ask the minister whether in his opinion gold mining is not inflation as far as prices go.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not know; I would have to give some thought to that. I do not know that I should like to give an opinion on that point offhand; I would have to try to see the real meaning of the question. Is the hon. gentleman suggesting that the production of gold which is exchanged for goods is more inflationary than the production of some other product which is exchanged for goods? Why would that be?

In the production of gold something like $200,000,000 of purchasing power is distributed; but gold is a substance which nobody uses and which is exchanged, I understand, to the United States for munitions of war, which of course the people here do not consume. The money distributed because of the production of gold is effective purchasing power, but there is no addition to the amount of retail goods to correspond with the increased purchasing power.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I see what the hon. gentleman means, but gold is no more exchanged for munitions than for fruits and vegetables or other consumer goods that are brought in from the United States. You cannot allocate gold to munitions any more than you can allocate it to farm machinery. I do not see that the production of gold can be put on a different footing from the production of any other commodity. We are not exchanging gold for United States munitions any more than we exchange other products, such as newsprint, that we export to the United States. I am unable to see why it is any more inflationary to produce gold than it is to produce newsprint or coarse grains.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
There has been a change
made in the regulations affecting exchange relative to fresh fruits and vegetables coming into Canada. When was this change made? What is
the extent of the exchange relaxation? Has the minister given consideration to the results of this change at this particular time? We are now entering a period when there is a great production in our own country of fresh fruits and vegetables, and I should like to know if the minister has given careful consideration to the results which may arise from this change and the freer entry of fruits and vegetables into Canada?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Prices are so high in the United States that I do not think there will be any effect at all. The timing was not very good. The recommendation was made by the wartime prices and trade board, but I think it was six weeks before it finally went through, because a lot of things had to be straightened out. Final action was not taken until June 22. While that was not too late to do any good, it was getting along toward the period when it would have been too late. We took off the war exchange tax and the special excise duty. The special excise duty of 3 per cent applies only to importations from countries against which the general tariff applies. In practice this will mean Mexico. It has been 10 per cent against the United States and 13 per cent against Mexico.
Does it apply to any fruits besides grapefruit?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
There are thirteen fruits and
vegetables covered.

Are they not nearly all
vegetables?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I think there are three or four fruits. I have not the list here.

Has the minister's
department carried on any negotiations with the Department of Munitions and Supply in connection with the bonus on fuel wood. Apparently the policy is to pay the dollar subsidy direct to the dealer. During last week-end I was in a part of the country where wood is the only fuel used, and I had an opportunity of talking to a great many men who make it their business to cut wood. I was informed that the people who actually cut the wood will get no benefit from this subsidy, that it goes to the dealer. This means that the dealer is getting an extra dollar profit on wood which someone else cuts. A number of these men told me that they have been in the habit of cutting wood and delivering it direct to customers. One man told me that he had delivered as many as a thousand cords of wood in a year without having it go through any retailer. He has been unable to get any part
War Appropriation-Labour

of this subsidy. Could not steps be taken to see that this subsidy is paid directly to the men who cut the wood? I do not think it will be possible to get an increase in the production of wood fuel unless some means can be adopted to shunt this dollar into the pockets of the men who actually do the cutting.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
That would come under
another department. I do not know very much about it and I am not in position to explain it. I believe the Minister of Munitions and Supply has dealt with the matter on several occasions.
He made it quite clear that it went to the dealer.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: And he gave some veiy good reasons why that would bring about the results, if I remember correctly. I do not want to cross wires with him; it is up to him to explain that.
I asked the minister for a break-down of this amount.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I will give that at eight o'clock.

Minister of Labour
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, when the estimates for the Department of Labour were before the committee I said that I would reply to a number of questions that had been asked by some hon. gentlemen.
I will deal first with the question asked by the hon. member for St. John-Albert, who asked me for a statement on the information division of the Department of Labour.
This branch was established in December, 1942. Previously, publicity work had been handled by various staffs-by a director of publicity and staff, under the director of national selective service; by a director of publicity for the Department of Labour proper, and by a director of publicity for the unemployment insurance commission. The new information division represented a consolidation of the work.
The duties of the information division consist of the preparation and issue of press releases, preparation of special articles on the work of the department, informational contacts, preparation and placing of paid advertising, and other duties as assigned.

The staff, and annual salaries, are now as follows:
1 director of information at	 $3,500
1 writer-translator at	 3,000
1 advertising specialist at	 2,820
1 principal clerk at	 1,920

These salaries are augmented by cost of living bonus up to but not including $3,000. At the moment an officer of the industrial relations branch at a salary of $3,120 is temporarily on loan with the information division.
Cost of operating the division since its establishment seven months ago amounts to $9,000, approximately, to June 15, 1943.
My hon. friend the leader of the opposition asked for information with respect to the records kept by the local employment selective service offices.
In the larger offices, a humber of telephone operators are in constant attendance in the order room, where telephone orders are received from the employers and full details noted on an employer's order card.
This card is then sent to the priority section of the office, where by use of the industrial classification manual published by the Department of Labour early in this year the classification number of the industry is placed on the card. I think this manual is a tribute to that section of the Department of Labour. In it will be found a classification of practically all the industrial occupations in Canada. I think this is the first time such a thing has ever been attempted in this country.
Will copies of the manual be available to hon. members?

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
speechtext: I will get the hon. member a copy.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Is it a new publication?

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
speechtext: It is a recent publication which we have got out for the guidance of selective service officers.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: How long has it been out?

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
speechtext: It was issued early this year. I do not say that I had something to do with its drafting, but I had something to do with the initial steps taken to develop a manual of this description.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Do not be too modest.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
speechtext:
I am just saying that
I am not responsible for drafting the manual. It will be appreciated by anyone who has any knowledge of the various classifications of

War Appropriation-Labour
industry how a manual of this sort can be of great assistance to people who may wish to consult it from time to time instead of relying on their memory.
Can we secure copies of it?

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
speechtext: I shall be glad to secure a copy for my hon. friend.
Thank you.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
speechtext:
From this number, reference is then made to the priority index, prepared by the inter-departmental committee on priorities, and the priority, whether (a) (b) (c) or (d), is marked on the employer's order card.
The card is then forwarded to that section of the office dealing with the particular industry, and there is placed in the live order file. The same procedure is followed in a more restricted form in the small offices.
When an applicant for work or a person directed to report to the office comes in, he is interviewed by a trained officer, and full particulars, such as his name, address, primary occupation, secondary occupation, age, height, weight, physical condition, disabilities, war service, education, specialized training, trade tests, farm experience and the nature of his previous employment experience, are all noted down on a card.
Some may ask why such particulars as height, weight and physical condition are required, but it will be readily understood that when men are wanted for heavy industries, for example, it is necessary to know something of the physical qualifications of those who are to be employed; that is why these particulars are noted on the questionnaire.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I suppose the officers
have to rely on the statement of the man himself as to his physical condition?

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
speechtext:
I would think so.
Under present conditions, when the demand for labour is so heavy, the bulk of the applicants can be immediately directed to an employer who is seeking their services, and for this purpose the national selective service permit form is issued and a notation made on the employer's order card that such and such a person has been referred to him.
It may be that upon the arrival of the applicant at the employer's place of business, the latter is unwilling to employ him. We have not yet reached the stage when we wish to compel an employer to hire a person who is unacceptable. Therefore, we always have on our records a large number-as of June 10 amounting to almost 40,000 persons-who are
what we describe as "unconfirmed referrals."
I would point out that in Great Britain the average number of "unconfirmed referrals" is about 100,000, and I understand the figure is higher in the United States, which probably has not yet reached the stage in the war that we have reached.
We are unable to prove that the person referred has actually been employed until we receive back from the employer the duplicate copy of the NSS permit, or check by telephone. The latter procedure has obvious limitations.
The situation may exist in certain localities where there are more applicants of a particular skill than we have employers' orders for. In this case, the same "application for employment" card is filled out and is filed on a live applicant file. That is what we call the live file. These files are constantly being examined by the officer concerned with that particular group of industries, with their related classes of occupation; and when an employer's order is received, applicants of the desired, qualifications are directed to the employer for interview in the order in which they made application. That is on the basis of seniority, which the hon. member for Vancouver East will understand probably as well as I do.
The persons are selected by means of the data which has already been collected and recorded on the "application for employment" card; and in all cases the applicant must necessarily be got in touch with a second time, in order that his national selective service permit may be made out. That is, he is given a permit to go to the employer. Then we have another check when he is there. A second form is then made out.
At this second interview, if there is any need for a further exhaustive examination into the previously recorded skills, the employment record or the personality of the individual, this is, of course, done at that time, and I make the point that very few jobs are changed on the basis of something which happens to be on a card.
In fact, no persons are being moved to new employment under the compulsory orders without a thorough examination having first been made into their previous experience and present capabilities. I think that will be readily understood. When you are moving men by compulsory order you must do everything that is humanly possible to see that they are suitable to the occupation to which they are being directed. We have had a number of complaints and have traced some of them

i
War Appropriation-Labour
down, and we found that where it seemed on the surface that perhaps some ridiculous action had been taken, after we looked into the matter we found that it was not as described in the press in certain instances.
We maintain in each local office an employer's record form which contains such essentials as name, address, plant unit, employer's number, principal product, name of personnel manager, normal working forces, male and female, agreements with trade unions, special skills utilized, a record of visits to the plant by our own officers, and a record of all transactions with the local office. That follows; the man who is in an insurable trade or calling naturally has his insurance book picked up and placed with the new employer.
The employer's order, form UIC 733, gives such information as the employer's name, address, business division of the firm, the occupations of the persons required, description of their duties, the rates of pay, regular and overtime, how often paid and when, hours of work per day, per week, probable duration of the work, the requirements as to experience, skill, age, et cetera; the tools-I should probably point out that some tradesmen carry all their tools and some carry part of their tools; some tools are provided by the employer-special equipment, permits, licences, certificates of educational standing, et cetera, which are required, the board and living conditions, the transportation arrangements, the person to whom the applicant should apply; and it makes provision on the back for details of the transactions covered under this order.
The priority form gives the division of industry and the number of the industry within that division, all of which is taken from the industrial classification manual published for the use of the employment offices, and also shows on the same card the priority rating, whether (a), (b), (c) or (d), the date at which it was authorized and separate ratings for men and women.
For the applicant's records, we have the form UIC /Oil which contains the details such as name, address, occupation, et cetera, which have already been enumerated; the NSS form 120, which is the separation notice given by the employer, the most recent copy of which is always maintained on the office files, and which contains, of course, written proof of the man's previous employment and his reason for separation.
The NSS form 122 is the permit to seek employment, two copies of which are handed to the applicant-one for his own use, and one, in postcard form, for the employer to return 
to the office as proof that he has employed the applicant-the third copy remaining on the office files.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Is there any difficulty with that part of the machinery?

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
speechtext:
I would not say so.
When you are handling the vast number of human beings that we are handling, I would say it works out reasonably well. Some are bound to slip through the net; I think that is natural, but as you gain more experience with this operation that kind of thing will become less and less.
There are other special forms which may be used from time to time, and special reports covering various industries, but the ones already mentioned are the basic and essential ones on which our employment service is based.
As to statistics, the first form which might be mentioned is form UIC 753A, which is the daily work sheet used by the local office to compile the statistical data required for form UIC 751A.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: May I ask the minister why some are UIC and some national selective service?

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
speechtext:
I do not know. I think
it is just as the thing develops. Personally I see no reason why all should not be selective service. I might point this out to my hon. friend: I think I know what is in his mind. The unemployment insurance commission was functioning before we thought of selective service, and1 they retained the name UIC. on the forms which were in use prior to the development of selective service. Personally I see no reason why we should not call them all by the same name, "selective service," except that when you are handling forms people get accustomed to using a particular name for them, and notwithstanding that you might change it, in the office routine they still use the same name.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: That would seem to indicate that the offices were still being manned by the original unemployment insurance personnel.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
speechtext:
Absolutely. As a matter of fact the whole selective service system has been built on the unemployment insurance offices, just as it has been in Great Britain, the United States, Australia, New Zealand, and any other country where they had that form of organization for what they call job placement. The selective service has been superimposed upon it. In every country that has been done.

War Appropriation-Labour
Form UIC 751A is a weekly report giving a great deal of information on the vacancies in stated' industries, at the beginning of the week, notified during the period, cancelled during the period, et cetera.
Also prepared1 at the local office is form UIC 757, showing the number of unfilled vacancies by industry priority, divided into approximately 100 separate occupations.
This form also shows the unconfirmed referrals to employers, that is, those applicants sent to employers for whom we have not yet received a confirmation by the receipt of the employer's copy of the NSS. permit, and also the numbers of unreferred applicants in each of these 100 or so occupations.
Just at that .point, how does the employer find out what is the priority, whether he is (a), (b), (c) or (d)?

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
speechtext: He does not find out.
Just at that point he does find out. My hon. friend's friend from Waterloo North gave an interview to the press stating that certain industries were in (b) priority. How did fte come to know ?

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
speechtext: I do not know. Who is "my hon. friend's friend"?'

The minister's friend from Waterloo North. He is in the chamber now, behind the curtains; perhaps he can explain how he gave an interview to the press some three or four weeks ago stating that a certain industry had a (b) priority.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
speechtext:
From these two reports which I have mentioned statistics are compiled for the whole of Canada at Ottawa showing the vacancies and referrals of males by priorities for all industries, in greater or lesser detail, as is required by the department. The same procedure is used for the preparation of reports for females.
All these forms have been amended and improved upon as a result of the greater amount of information required, and the more rigid control of employment which we have instituted.
For years, however, a record of the vacancies and of the placements as reported to us, both by the old provincial employment offices, and since July, 1941, by the offices operated under the jurisdiction of the unemployment insurance commission, has been published in the Labour Gazette.
I should like to lay on the table copies of the following forms:
1.	Employer's record card, form UIC 731.
2.	Employer's order-male, form UIC 733.
3.	The priority form.
4.	Industrial classification manual.
5.	Employee's application for employment, form UIC 701.

My hon. friend the leader of the opposition asked for a statement as to the resignations, since the resignation of the former director of selective service, of certain gentlemen employed by selective service.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Some seventeen, I think. The minister is going to read the names?

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
speechtext: Yes; I will put it all on the record.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Can we have the dates of the resignations?

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
speechtext:
I have not them here, but if my hon. friend wants them I can get them for him. He did not ask for the dates, but there is no reason why I should not give them.

Campbell, L. S.; consultant, resigned to take a more remunerative position.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Were these the reasons the department give for their resignations?

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
speechtext:
Absolutely. I would say this to my hon. friend. I am not placing any blame; but a good many men were hired without consultation with anyone; when it was necessary to keep the record straight they were gone over by the civil service commission, and certain allowances were dropped and certain classifications established, and some of these gentlemen, naturally, did
War Appropriation-Labour

not agree with their classification, and resigned. The Department of Labour as such had no jurisdiction in the matter. But that was done, and from my own point of view it had to be done; may I say that.
Garside, S. T.: consultant; resigned because of discontinuance of arrangement to pay living expenses when away from Toronto, in addition to salary.
Grabill, E. L.: chief enforcement officer, Montreal, classification out of line with other enforcement positions in the service as approved by treasury board and civil service commission. Resigned on account of reduction in salary.
Harvey, Robert: executive assistant. Returned to Allied War Supplies Limited, from which corporation he had been on loan.
Holland, L.: consultant-was in charge of staff personnel. Resigned, reason not stated.
Melancon, Claude: publicity director. Returned to Canadian National Railways, from the staff of which he had been on loan on the understanding that period of loan would be limited.
Perhaps I might state a personal experience I had when we organized the national war labour board. Sometimes it is necessary to borrow a man for six or nine months, and in one case Mr. E. R. Complin, of Canadian Industries Limited, came as an executive director of the national war labour board, Mr. G. W. Huggett, president and general manager, having very kindly loaned him to the department until we could get over the hump-and get the thing on paper. It was more or less an administrative undertaking and we borrowed him for six months. After that he went back to Canadian Industries Limited.
McGillivray, L.: news and feature writer. Resigned in order to take a position with wartime prices and trade board.
McTaggart, K.: news and feature writer. Resigned to return to newspaper work.
Quinn, Valentine: selective service officer. It was not found possible to assign him to a position at a salary he felt he should receive, and in consequence his services were dispensed with.
There is nothing new about that; you get it in all business and governmental organizations.
Reinke, Carl: assistant to director. Resigned. No reason given.
Roberts, W. R.: consultant. Transferred to a position with the timber controller.
Smith, Goldwyn: consultant. Resigned due to personal dissatisfaction with status on the staff of national selective service, stating he was to return to his former position in the university of Iowa.

Taylor, Robert: news and feature writer. Resigned to return to the press gallery.
Wright, L. A.: assistant director. Resigned to return to Engineering Institute of Canada of which he is secretary.
I think my hon. friend will agree with me that these things happen in every business organization-resignations because salaries are not good enough, and that sort of thing. I am frank to admit that a good deal of publicity has been given the matter. In a well-known national newspaper in this province there appeared a leading article on the resignation of one of the officials of external affairs, who was loaned to us for a short period in the formative stages of the establishment of selective Service. I refer to Mr. John Deutsch. This is the letter written to Mr. MacNamara by Mr. Norman A. Robertson in this connection: Dear Mr. MacNamara:
With reference to our correspondence and conversations about the services of Mr. John Deutsch, I wish to confirm my understanding that Mr. Deutsch will return to the Department of External Affairs on Monday, January 18. I am sorry that I am not in a position to make his services available to your department for a longer period, but the pressure of work on the economic side of this department makes his return impeftitive. I need not add that he and his colleagues in the department on the economic and prisoners of war side of the work will always be ready to help where they can in dealing with aspects of these questions which are of concern to both our departments.
Yours sincerely,
N. A. Robertson.
I know Mr. Deutsch quite well. We borrowed him for two or three months from external affairs until we got over the preliminary work of laying down the administrative policy in connection with selective service, and after that period he went back to where he had come from.

Then, as a main reason possibly for having prices fixed as they are, he said that if prices were raised we would have to have a general increase in wages. If there were an increase in farm wages I think there would not be any complaint, because to-day farm help is lower paid than the help in any other industry in Canada. The object of the
activities of the whole wartime prices and trade board set-up and the object of this proposed expenditure of $120,000,000 is, I take it, to prevent inflation in Canada. Will the minister agree that that is the object?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is part of our programme.

The object is to prevent inflation. There has been a good deal of misunderstanding of the meaning of the word "inflation" in the house, and there is still a good deal of misunderstanding about it in the country. We have heard members of the house use the word "inflation" with a variety of meanings. I believe it is very important to the progress of this country and the progress of the world that every member of this committee get clearly into his mind that inflation is a rise in price.

Another
lecture.
The hon. member for York-Sunbury needs ten lectures, and then he would not know.

I feel
flattered at the testimonial just given me by the member for Lethbridge, because I venture to say that ninety per cent of the members of this house are in the same position with me, so that I feel I am in good company.

It is all the more
reason why we should stop and discuss this matter with some care at this very time, because until we understand what inflation is, it will be impossible for this country to accomplish any of the things we are aiming to accomplish in the peace, and it will be impossible for the world to accomplish the fine things which are envisaged in the Atlantic charter.
The meaning of inflation is fundamental to an understanding of economics. I would like to commend the minister and the wartime prices and trade board for the great amount of activity in which they have been engaged and for the great many discoveries which they have made. They are being more or less forced into making important discoveries. The minister is doing things this year which two and a half years ago he would have considered quite impossible. A few minutes ago he rather wanted to lecture me because
I was going to talk theoretically, but in the last two and a half years the minister has learned a lot of theory he did not know before, and I promise him that if he will keep as alert in the next two years and a half as he has been in the last two and a half he will learn a whole lot more than he possibly imagines now.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Not to-night, though!

No; I would not
undertake to teach the minister to-night. What I am concerned about is that we understand that inflation is merely a rise in price and that inflation can be prevented by devices similar to those which are being used by the wartime prices and trade board at the present time.
I wish to refer for a moment or two to the question I raised just before the dinner recess as to why it would not be possible to raise the price of agricultural products by subsidies without making it necessary for the labouring man to receive higher wages. The minister expressed considerable anxiety, saying that it would put into circulation a great deal of purchasing power which would have an inflationary tendency.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
There is another reason,
too, namely, the tremendous administrative difficulties involved in subsidy payments. At the moment we are having so much difficulty with some of the payments that we feel we may have to stop them just for administrative reasons.

The administrative
difficulties are great, but the minister wall be the first to acknowledge that Canada, with all the administrative difficulties which she has assumed, is in a far healthier condition than the United States where they have refrained from assuming the responsibility of going through such difficulties. It will be discovered by and by, when men know more about money and prices and kindred matters, that there are simple techniques which can be used which avoid many of the administrative difficulties.
But let me go back to the question which the minister raised. He said that if we put a good deal more money into circulation, it would have an inflationary tendency. But it will not matter how much inflationary tendency there is if prices are controlled.
Prices can be controlled in three different ways. One is by definite price fixing; another is by subsidies such as the wartime prices and trade board is using in many directions, and another is by rationing. These three

devices wisely and scientifically used will control inflation. There may be administrative difficulties; we are bound to have. difficulties because we are trying to use an outmoded financial system that we should never be trying to use. We are trying to bolster up a ramshackle thing, and of course we are having all the difficulties that a person would have in trying to run a fifteen year old car in comparison with one who is trying to run a car which has just come out of the factory. That is why the difficulties are so numerous; we are trying to use an outmoded system, an ox-cart system which -we should have discarded long ago. May I repeat that prices of agricultural products could be raised by subsidies and bonuses very much like those which are used to-day, and there would be no necessity for a rise in the price of agricultural products to the general consumer any more than there is for a rise in the price of milk, which rise the minister has taken great care to prevent. Society as a whole has absorbed the rise, so that the consumer does not have to pay. That is the first point that I wish to make.
May I repeat once more that inflation is simply a rise in prices. Now, if inflation is a rise in price, I wonder if it will be worth while to direct the committee's attention-I believe I will-to this fact. If inflation is only a rise in price, and if it can be prevented by subsidies of one sort or another, is there any reason why state-created debt-free money could not be used for the subsidies just as well as the money which is now being used? If there is any reason, it would be a good thing to have it immediately.

I have said before in this house several times until I have wearied the hon. member for York-Sunbury-bless his soul; men like him we need for ballast-I have said time and again, until many hon. members have grown weary of the thing, that money could be created. I have pointed out that in the last war Canada created $26,000,000 worth of bills. The treasury board did it; they printed the money; there was no debt attached to it at all. He asked whether there was any sufficient reason why wholesale and systematic rationing should be more difficult in Canada than it is in Great Britain.
The essential element in any rationing scheme is effective control of supplies, and in this respect the British rationing authorities, especially in the field of food rationing, are in many instances in a much more advantageous position than is the wartime prices and trade board in Canada.
As examples of some of the major differences between the two countries I would point to the following:
1.	The larger number of producers of foodstuffs in Canada scattered over a much greater physical area.
2.	A large proportion of the United Kingdom's food supplies are imported and the British Ministry of Food is thus enabled to obtain complete control over these supplies to the extent of owning them. In Canada, on the other hand, the board is forced to meet the situation where certain of the important foods to be rationed-for example, meat, butter-are domestically produced by a large number of small producers, with the result that control of supplies is necessarily less effective.
3.	In part because of the smaller size of the country and the less diversified character of its agriculture, the British Ministry of Food has been able to exercise stringent measures of control over farmers which have not been considered practicable for introduction in Canada. This greater measure of control, supplementing the control exercised by government purchase of food imports, is carried to the extent that the Ministry of Food owns the live cattle which are slaughtered. I would point out, for example, that farmers in Britain must give twelve days' notice prior to slaughtering, and animals may be slaughtered only in government-controlled abattoirs, while the number of abattoirs allowed to be operated has been reduced by ninety-five per cent.
4.	Because of the larger physical area of Canada it is impossible to have a standard price structure throughout the country for basic food commodities. The fact that the British Ministry of Food has been able to

establish such a standard set of prices for meat has allowed it to ration meat on a value basis, thus freeing it from much of the complication of the points plan which has had to be adopted for Canada.
5.	Consumption habits are more uniform in Britain than in Canada, and coupon rationing whereby everyone is entitled to an equal quantity of the rationed article or articles is, therefore, more suitable in Britain than in Canada. It is necessary in Canada to take account of differences in consumption due to such things as occupation or geography and this is very difficult to achieve under rationing.
That is the answer to the question the hon. gentleman asked the other night. I am not prepared to go further at the moment.
