I wonder if the minister would look into it, because it has been contended that the housing situation in both Vancouver and New Westminster would be helped if the conversion value were reduced to, say $3,500 or $4,000, which would take in about eighty per cent of the homes in both cities.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: If the hon. gentleman is thinking about the same thing I am thinking about, he is thinking about big buildings. I am thinking about the housing conversion plan, which is a new plan for converting large houses into apartments. The object is to get as many family units as possible out of one building. It is expected that family units can be obtained at the cost of $1,000 to $1,500. provided enough apartments can be made out of one house. My impression would be that if a house were only worth, to start with $3,000 or $4,000, it would not be an appropriate building to come under the housing conversion plan.

It will take only a mpment to read the brief which was presented in the matter. It is very short:
Recently the government appointed a real property administrator, and under the order in council, he was empowered to take over any premises of any nature that might be utilized for war purposes, or for use of those employed in any war enterprise. A short while after this appointment a new regulation was passed which nullified for the duration of the war any local municipality or province acts of regulations, restricting housing occupancy. In so far as Vancouver was concerned this could possibly be implied to nullify the Shaughnessy restriction act, which provides that this area could only be used as a one-family dwelling district. Under this amendment it is now possible for all houses in this district to be used for rooming or boarding houses, or made into multiple dwellings, or made into two or more apartments. The effect of this regulation in regard to the Shaughnessy area, along with the proposal to limit the expense of conversion to $1,500, would virtually change that area into a somewhat slum condition, as the houses are so laid out, and of such a character, that with an expenditure of only $1,500 there would be such a contrast to the original structure and finish that they would become a second or third class accommodation.
[Mr. Reid.3
The intention of the government in restricting the housing conversion to dwellings of a market value of $7,000 or over, is utterly impractical as far as Vancouver is concerned, as the vast majority of these houses are either in Shaugh-nessy, South West Marine, or British Properties on the north shore. The houses most suitable for conversion are in the $3,000 to $6,000 class.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That may be so, but the brief my hon. friend has just read is a pretty good argument for not going into the small house. The writer says that it will cost more than SI,500 to get your units, and the government is interested in getting a cheap unit. We can get them for $1,000 under proper conditions. If you get the right kind of big old house, you can convert it into ten or a dozen apartments. That is a cheap way to get family units. You have to get the right type of house, of course, and make the right kind of bargain with the owner. An order in council was passed authorizing the conversion of, I think, fifty buildings in Vancouver. Mr. Nichols, the director of housing, who is doing the administrative part of the work, went to British Columbia and I thought he was making pretty satisfactory progress but on a limited scale. We cannot go in for it in a wholesale way. It would be expensive, and as the writer says, it might make slums out of good houses if you started in on cheap houses.
I understood the ninister to offer to give me an answer, and I 3laim the right, Mr. Chairman, to have the answer before the item is carried.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
There is a special order about the Vancouver area. It is order 238 of the wartime prices and trade board. Section 4 reads:
4. The price to be paid to primary producers for milk delivered to a milk dealer's or producer-distributor's plant for sale by the dealer or producer-distributor in the Vancouver area in the form of milk, cream or ice cream shall be as follows, according to quantity and butter fat content:
(a)	for each 100 pounds of milk of 3-5 per cent butter fat content, $2.45;
(b)	for each 100 pounds of milk, the butter fat content of which is greater or less than 3-5 per cent, $2.45 plus or minus 5 cents for each one-tenth of one per cent of butter fat content greater or less, as the case may be, than 3-5 per cent;
(c)	for milk in quantities of less than 100 pounds, a price proportionate according to quantity to the prices stated in clauses (a) and (b) above for the quantity of 100 pounds.
I said a while ago that there was no ceiling on the sale, but there seems to be a special order applicable to the Vancouver area, to ensure a price to producers comparable to that prevailing in similar markets elsewhere in Canada.

War Appropriation-Prices Stabilization

I appreciate the answer which the minister has given, and I think Hansard will bear me out in the argument I advanced. This is once, Mr. Chairman, that I wish I followed the practice of some of my friends from Ontario of reading a speech, but I never have and I never will read what I have to say so long as I am in the House of Commons. I will say my speech as I think it.
Approximately seventy-five per cent of the producers of milk in the province of British Columbia are in the Fraser valley. They sell twenty-five per cent of their milk on the fluid market, and anybody who knows the dairy industry knows that that is where the money is. They sell the rest, seventy-five per cent, in manufactured products.
My information is, and I think this is borne out by the minister's statement to-night, representing the wartime prices and trade board which comes under his department, that the price is set to the wholesalers on what we can sell the distributors. As I said, we produce seventy-five per cent of the milk and we sell, in round figures, twenty-five per cent of our milk on the fluid market and the other seventy-five per cent on what is known as the open market, which means the world market, in the form of cheese, butter and byproducts. The other twenty-five per cent of the producers sell 100 per cent of their milk on the fluid market, where the money is, and yet as I understand the minister and the regulations, the wartime prices and trade board say to us who are the wholesalers that we must sell to the distributors at a certain price. For the sake of argument we will say that it is $2.50 per 100 pounds of 3-5 per cent milk. We are not allowed to charge more than that. We are not allowed to pay our own retail outlets more. We who represent seventy-five per cent of the dairy producers in British Columbia are not allowed to pay our producers more than that set price, and we as wholesalers pay that as distributors.
In our own particular case we own both companies. But the price is set by the wartime prices and trade board. We cannot pay our own distributors any more than that. I suggest to you, Mr. Chairman, that the reason why the price is fixed in that way is that there is a small minority of independent distributors who must depend upon us as wholesole distributors for the volume of fluid milk for sale, and for that reason and that reason only the price is kept at this minimum. I am using the figure of $2.50 per 100 pounds for the sake of argument. In our particular case we represent seventy-five per cent of the dairy
producers. We own our own wholesale and our own retail outlets. I do not know whether I am making myself clear to the minister, but those are the regulations as I understand them, and as I understood the minister to confirm them to-night. The minister has all the details. My interpretation of the act is that we as wholesalers sell to the independent distributors at a given price and must sell at that price.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The price to the primary
producer, if he delivers the milk to a milk dealer's plant or a producer-distributor's plant, for sale by the dealer or the producer-distributor, in the Vancouver area, in the form of milk, cream or ice cream is set at the figures I have mentioned. That is all I can tell my hon. friend. I put the section on Hansard and I think it is clear enough.

I appreciate what
the minister said in reference to the section, and all that, but I have no recourse but to do what I am now doing, because I am deprived of the right to do it in the committee on agriculture. I want to know who advised that this price was to be set as it is_that we as wholesalers, representing the producers, must sell to the independent distributors at a given price.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The date of this order is
February 16, 1943. It is dated just after Mr. Taggart left the office of foods administrator, and I am informed that he worked out the order. He was very familiar with conditions in British Columbia, I know, because he used to talk about conditions in the Fraser valley, and I believe he sent a man out there to work out this order. I do not know whom he consulted out there. Perhaps he consulted my hon. friend. Did he?

I wish he had. I think the minister knows that I do not want to delay matters. If I were one of those who want to do that, I could rise in my place and spend time as a farm representative telling the Minister of Finance many things. He is the greatest Minister of Finance we have ever had, a man we all look up to and admire. He knows I am not making a personal issue of this. I am speaking as the representative of a section of the people-and do not forget this, that I have never read a speech in this house. I speak without reading, and what I say goes back to the people of my district from myself and not from the maritimes. I think I am entitled to the information I am seeking. In our district we own our own wholesale outfit, which is the largest cooperative dairy organization in Canada and the
4550	COMMONS
War Appropriation-Prices Stabilization
second largest on the north American continent. That is something that can be verified. We also control our own retail outlet. Now I want to be corrected if I am wrong, and that is the minister's job, because I am not allowed to find it out in the committee on agriculture. My information is that our own wholesale outfit, which we own, is not allowed to sell to our own retail outlet except at a certain figure set by the wartime prices and trade board. Is that right?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am afraid I cannot tell my hon. friend that.

Will the minister produce some member of the wartime prices and trade board before me who can answer that question? I want to repeat it. My information is that the price which the associated dairies association can pay to the Fraser valley milk producers' association is set by the wartime prices and trade board. That is my information. Before the item is carried I am entitled to the information in that regard, and so far as I am concerned, before this item is carried I shall know whether the wartime prices and trade board sets the price to the farmer organization owned by the farmers, the price at which they can sell to their own retail organization, about fifty-three per cent of which is owned by the farmers. Is that correct, or is that price which is to be paid by the distributors set by certain independent companies?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: How would it do for the hon. gentleman to get in touch with the foods administrator, to-morrow say, and get this information then?
Mr. Chairman, I have been trying for three weeks to do that.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: There is no difficulty about it.

I know there is no difficulty in getting in touch with them'-and very fine gentlemen they are, too. I have met them. But the minister knows as well as I do that the only place where anything effective can be done for the farmers is in this chamber. I cannot get my point before the committee on agriculture. I have tried for three weeks, and they refuse to hear me.
I ask the minister this straight question: Has a wholesale company or cooperative to conform, on their sale to their own distributors
a price set by the wartime prices and trade board? If so, why?

Mr. Chairman, I know something about the milk business, and I think I can answer the hon. member from British Columbia. There are regulations in

his province, the same as in all provinces of Canada. I am not sure whether they have a milk commission in British Columbia, but I know we have in Quebec. These commissions were formed to protect the farmers against themselves. Formerly, when farmers retailed their milk they tried to cut each other's throats. Finally the provincial government appointed a commission to set the price. That price was set after interviewing the different farmer organizations in my province. They are not allowed to pay less than the commission price, and they are obliged to sell at the price stipulated.
I believe the farmers are fairly well satisfied at the present time. I am in direct touch with them every day when I am at home, and I know conditions are far better than they were before the war. Unfortunately for the farmers, prices of butter and cheese are not set according to the cost of production. That is too bad for the farmers, but it has always been that way-and especially so before the war. Now the government is giving a bonus of 8 cents on butter, and about the same thing in proportion for cheese. Only the other day a farmer came to me and said that while he had only a small herd he had received $75 from his creamery, that he had never got that much before and that he was well satisfied. Before the war farmers were obliged to take 18 to 20 cents a pound for butterfat. Now we are paying them 46 or 47 cents, and they are fairly happy about it. Perhaps that is not very high, but certainly it is much better than they got before. There was some difficulty last winter in connection with securing grain, and now they are having some trouble in getting hired help. But had it not been for those two things I think everything would be very satisfactory for the farmers. If my hon. friend wishes to have some other information, I should be glad to give it to him.

Mr. Chairman, I appreciate the lecture by the hon. member from Quebec, and I am very glad to know the Quebec farmers are satisfied. But I am perfectly entitled to say that the British Columbia farmers are not satisfied. If my hon. friend is satisfied with the treatment given the dairy farmers of Quebec, then it is all right for him to say so, and I have no quarrel with his opinion. But we in British Columbia are not satisfied. I should not have to .tell why we are not. We never will /pay the wages, or have the social security enjoyed by the province of Quebec.
I have asked a question. Might I point out in passing that the Minister of Agriculture himself-and there is no better authority on

War Appropriation-
-Prices Stabilization
agriculture on the north American continent -has admitted that it costs us more in British Columbia to produce than it does in the hon. member's native province of Quebec. Incidentally I might point out, for the benefit of a few, that so far we have done very well for the legal profession, and for the privy council, a few times. But let me ask this: Are we to be allowed to sell our own wholesale milk to our own distributing agency? The hon. member from the Okanagan valley knows about this condition, and other hon. members from British Columbia know the circumstances. Are we to be allowed to sell our own milk from our own wholesale agencies, owned and controlled 100 per cent by the farmers, to our own retail agencies, at a price which we set? Now, mark you, I am not asking to upset the ceiling price of 11 cents a quart or whatever it is. I am talking about our own distributing agencies-and there is a big difference in that. We are not upsetting the retail price to the consumer in Vancouver, Victoria, or wherever it may be, even by one cent. All we are asking in this instance is for the privilege of selling to our own distributing agency or any other distributor at the price we see fit to set. I am asking the minister if we are to be permitted to do that, and I repeat that we are not upsetting the retail price to the consumer one iota. Are we to have the privilege of selling our surplus milk either to our own distributor, which in this instance is known as the Associated Dairies, or to whoever wishes to buy our milk, at our price?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall the item carry?
No, no; I object to this carrying stuff. I have asked the minister a question, and I speak for the 4,300 farmers I represent.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I have before me an order. I do not know the names or the set-up of the organization in the Fraser valley, As I read this order, it would seem to me that the wholesale organization comes within the definition of a primary producer, and the price which that wholesale organization can charge for milk is fixed! by this order. I should say, after reading this order, that if it is a sale to a dealer or a producer-distributor, it is governed by the provisions of the order. That is, if it is a sale. The hon. member is talking as if it is merely a family arrangement of some kind, and not a sale at all. He may be raising some fine legal point. He is asking me to say what this order does, or what it can do. He is asking what can be done legally. There is no doubt under this order that if it is a sale by a wholesale organization such as he has named-and I do not
know whether the one he has named is an incorporated body or not-but if it is a sale from that wholesaler to a milk dealer or producer-distributor, it is governed by the provisions of this order.
He can find out in ten minutes by asking an official of the wartime prices and trade board. I am informed there are several officials who have been out there and who understand this situation thoroughly. He can find that out by calling them by telephone tomorrow morning. All I can do is cite the order to him. Does he not know about this himself? Has this matter not been discussed since last February? Are the facts not well known? Does he not know that the price that the wholesale organization can charge is fixed? What is the object of this? Is the hon. gentleman asking me for a legal interpretation of the order, or is he asking me to tell him something he already knows, for the purpose of the record?
I do not have to worry about the record at all.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Then why does the hon. gentleman not go to the board to-morrow morning and get his information, instead of taking u>p all this time?

I am not going to be lectured by the minister or anybody else; I came here to represent the farmers of my riding. I first asked for this information in the agriculture committee. I know exactly what the minister has told me, but there is something else I am trying to bring home to him. I will tell him why I am asking these questions. The representatives of the wartime prices and trade board went out to British Columbia, Did they get in touch with the organization that represents at least seventy-five per cent of the dairy farmers of that province? No; they went to the other twenty-five per cent. I am here to do my duty as I see it, and if I do not do it I am quite prepared, if and when the time comes, to resign or to accept the decision of the voters of the constituency of Fraser Valley.
The minister has not yet answered my question. He has admitted that his department is afraid of the majority and is ko-towing to the minority in British Columbia. That was exactly what I said. Our own farmers sell to a wholesale organization known as the Fraser Valley Milk Producers' Association, who in turn sell to an organization known as Associated Dairies. I will admit that the minister has no reason to know all these details, but I want to tell the minister that the officials of the board are afraid to appear

War Appropriation-Prices Stabilization
before any committee, because as soon as they arrive in British Columbia they go to the minority group, get their instructions and report back to the wartime prices and trade board. His officials are afraid to appear before the committee and answer questions in that regard.
As the regulation stands to-day we have to pay a certain price; that has been admitted by the minister. It does not make a particle of difference to me if the minister shrugs his shoulders; I can shrug mine, too. I represent 4,300 dairymen. Our organization has to sell milk, through a wholesale outfit to our own distributors at a given price. Why? To protect this little minority of distributors who have been the godsend of the legal profession of British Columbia for the last fifteen years.
Carried.

Never mind the "carried" stuff. I should like to know if some of those hon. members who call "carried" are satisfied with prices of dairy products in Ontario. Certainly we in British Columbia are not satisfied, and we are not afraid to say so. Will the minister tell me why we cannot set our own price to our own distributors, provided-and I want this to be quite clear-that we keep within the ceiling price to the consumer? I understand the purpose of these regulations is to protect the consumer, and I admire the excellent work the minister has done in that regard. All we are asking is that we be allowed to set our own price to the distributors, always keeping [DOT] within the retail price ceiling to the consumer. Are we or are we not to be allowed that privilege?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Did the hon. member ask why they should not be allowed to do something? What was his question?

My question is: will we be permitted, as wholesalers, to sell to our own distributors at any price we see fit, or to any other distributors, provided the ceiling price to the consumer is not disrupted?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not think you can, under this order.

Well, Mr. Chairman, I imagine I am not making myself very clear. I know we cannot do it under the present order. I am not afraid of being quoted as saying that in this instance I represent seventy-five per cent of the dairymen of Fraser valley.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Who represents the other twenty-five per cent?
I see I shall have to talk until eleven o'clock to get this across, but I am asked who represents the other twenty-five per cent.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries
speechtext: Nobody questions that.
No? A few years ago we were told that we could not produce enough fish. We put away 1,800 Japanese fishermen and to-day we are producing more fish in British Columbia than we ever produced.
Milk is the item.

The Minister of
Fisheries asked for that. I am pointing out that I represent seventy-five per cent of the daiiymen of the Fraser valley, and I think I am putting up a reasonable argument; I believe the hon. member for New Westminster will bear me out. I have not been able to get an answer as yet. Through you, Mr. Chairman, I want to repeat that I was not allowed to bring up this matter in the agriculture committee, where it should be brought up, because they were afraid to face it.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Order, Mr. Chairman.

Never mind the
order; you cannot take it. Representing this percentage of the dairymen, all I am asking is that as wholesalers of milk we be given the right to state to the distributors what the price shall be, as long as it does not disrupt the price ceiling. A moment ago the minister said he could not answer that suggestion. Well, Mr. Chairman, if I cannot approach the matter through the Minister of Finance, who is head of the wartime prices and trade board, through whom in the name of time can I approach it? I cannot approach it through the Minister of Agriculture; he says he has nothing to do with the setting of that price, which I admit. Let me repeat that we do not want to disrupt the ceiling price to the consumer by one iota. We want the privilege of saying what the price from the producer to the distributor shall be. I say to the minister, through you, Mr. Chairman-the hon. member for New Westminster was called to order for not addressing the Chair - that approximately seventy-five per cent of the dairymen of the province cannot produce milk at the present price to the consumer. They want to increase the price to the distributor by five or seven cents per pound butterfat, but by order of the board they are refused that right. I want to repeat under the ruling of the board we are refused the right as wholesalers to increase our price

War Appropriation-Prices Stabilization
to the distributors and keep within the ceiling price to the consumer. Are the rights of democracy, are the rights of the majority to be considered, or are the rights of the minority to be considered? As soon as the board's dairy representative arrived in British Columbia he approached the twenty-five per cent, not the seventy-five per cent. He is afraid to appear before the agriculture committee. I ask the minister again, and I want an answer; if I have to talk for four days I can do so. Can the wholesaler of milk set the price to his own distributor or any distributor, provided the retail price does not exceed the price as set by the wartime prices and trade board?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Why do they wish to lower the price to the distributors?
Lower it?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I know the hon. member for Fraser Valley does not want to prolong the debate unduly. He has always been most fair. I think he realizes that the Minister of Finance and his officials are not backward in answering any questions. I think he realizes that the minister has tried to answer in the best way possible, and I ask the hon. member to take that answer.
I appreciate your generous decision, Mr. Chairman, but the minister has asked me a direct question. I am flattered, because this is the first time I have been asked a question by so eminent a person.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Does the hon. gentleman wish to lower or raise it?

Now who is prolonging the debate? The minister has asked me a direct question. With all due deference to you, Mr. Chairman, I think the next time I shall write out my speech because I am about the only member who does not read what he has to say. We do not want to lower the price; we most decidedly want to raise it. I am asking why we as producers as represented by our own association-I mentioned the approximate figure of seventy-five per cent-and the present attorney general of British Columbia and the former attorney general of British Columbia, who now has the distinguished honour of having a seat in the place known as the other place-
Out of order.

It is not out of older. They have taken it to the privy council. We are saying that as the Fraser Valley Milk Producers' Association we have
the right to set the price at which milk is sold to the distributors, provided the cost to the ultimate consumer does not exceed the ceiling price. I am asking the minister if that is possible. I appreciate the fact that he cannot answer offhand.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Why does the hon. gentleman want to raise the price even to his own organization? That is what he has been talking about all evening.
The reason why I want to raise the price is that we sell seventy-five per cent of our milk to distributors.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: To your own distributors.
To our own distributors and others.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: To your own people. Why do you wish to raise it?

The remainder of our milk, the seventy-five per cent, goes into canned milk or manufactured milk-I am speaking in round figures-and twenty-five per cent goes into fluid milk. But 100 per cent of the milk produced by the other twenty-five per cent, the independent producers, goes into the fluid market. They cannot handle their consumers, so that they have to buy from our wholesalers, and we cannot charge them the price which our own distributing .agents are prepared to pay. This official of the wartime prices and trade board arrived in Vancouver, and he went down to this agency and asked what they could afford to pay.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The hon. gentleman is not interested in the price he is charging his own organization; all he is interested in is the price to be charged the independents. He wants to raise the price to the independents. Is that the idea?
No, I do not.
Eleven o'clock.
I happen to have the floor. Since I have not been able to make my point clear, I ask you, Mr. Chairman, to call it eleven o'clock.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall the item carry?
Carried.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall I report progress?
Is the item carried? I did not agree with that at all.

No; it was not carried.
Progress reported.

speechtext:
At eleven o'clock the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to standing order.
